Katalog Berita (Halaman 9/57)

#9640. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.

For inspiration, explore Michael Wagner’s voice-controlled VR demo or Maziyar Panahi’s Microduck simulation. Both show how developers are using SimReady assets in their own projects.

#9637. SuperDial Hits 10 Million AI Calls to Insurers and Now Wants to Make the Calls Unnecessary

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

Somewhere in the United States right now, a billing specialist is on hold with an insurance company, waiting to ask a question whose answer already sits on a screen. Multiply that call by millions and you get one of the most expensive habits in American healthcare. McKinsey estimated that simplifying healthcare administration could save up to $265 billion a year, more than a quarter of the roughly $950 billion the country spent on administration in 2019.

Automation is already chipping away at that bill. Electronic transactions helped US healthcare avoid $258 billion in administrative costs in 2024, while more than half of health plans now use AI in their administrative workflows. A new problem is emerging as a result. AI agents now sit on both ends of the phone line, with providers' bots calling payers' bots to ask for information that lives in a database.

SuperDial, whose AI agents handle payer communication for revenue cycle teams, has now completed more than 10 million AI-powered calls to insurers. The milestone has led the company to an unusual conclusion for a business built on automating phone calls: the next breakthrough is making those calls unnecessary. On 17th November, it introduced Agent-to-Agent RCM, an approach that measures success by resolved requests, not completed calls.

McKinsey's estimate breaks the $265 billion opportunity into three layers. About $175 billion could come from changes inside individual organizations, $35 billion from better coordination between organizations and $105 billion from industry-wide changes such as shared standards, with some overlap between the last two. That means about two-thirds of the savings sits within the reach of single providers and payers acting on their own. (our analysis)

Much of that spending flows through revenue cycle management, or RCM, the work of turning patient care into payment. It covers checking a patient's eligibility and benefits, securing prior authorization, following up on claims and keeping provider records current with each insurer. Every one of those steps requires information from a payer. Much of it still moves by phone, fax and web portal.

The 2025 CAQH Index, which tracks administrative transactions across more than 600 provider organizations and health plans covering 63% of insured lives, shows the industry is getting faster. Electronic transactions helped avoid $258 billion in administrative costs in 2024, up 17%, while medical administrative spending fell 9%. Electronic prior authorization rose from 31% to 40% between the 2023 and 2025 Index reports, while dental claim payments moved from 21% to 33%.

AI is accelerating that shift. More than half of health plans and a quarter of provider organizations now use AI tools in administrative workflows, while about two in three physicians used AI in some form by early 2025. CAQH still sees about $21 billion in savings available from automating the transactions that remain manual or partly manual.

The burden falls hardest on clinics. The American Medical Association's latest survey of 1,000 physicians found that practices handle an average of 40 prior authorizations a week, consuming 13 hours of physician and staff time, or about 1.6 working days (our arithmetic). Two in five practices employ staff who work only on prior authorization.

The cost reaches patients. 95% of physicians say prior authorization delays access to necessary care, while 79% report that patients abandon treatment because of authorization hurdles. Six in ten physicians also worry that AI on the payer side could raise denial rates, a sign that automation on one side of the system does not automatically help the other.

SuperDial's AI agents place calls on behalf of providers and billing companies, navigating phone trees, waiting on hold and talking to payer representatives to retrieve benefits, prior authorization and claim information. The company passed more than 1 million calls at the time of its $15 million Series A in June 2025, led by SignalFire with Slow Ventures, BoxGroup and Scrub Capital. It has now crossed 10 million, a tenfold rise in about 17 months (our analysis).

The platform serves provider groups, health systems, RCM companies and payers. It automates eligibility and benefits verification, prior authorization, claims follow-up, credentialing, enrollment and provider data management across phone, payer portals, EDI, APIs, fax and documents, then returns structured results to customers' systems. West Coast Dental has used it for more than 10,000 claim-status calls a month, while billing teams have reported up to 4x productivity gains.

AI has arrived on both sides of the transaction. Providers deploy agents to chase claim and benefit information, while payers deploy automation to answer those requests. Each side is getting better at keeping the exchange going. Neither is getting better at ending it, which risks automating the very inefficiency the industry set out to remove.

SuperDial's answer is to stop treating the phone call as the unit of work. If an agent already has information, that context should travel with the request. If a digital channel can supply the answer, there should be no call at all. The company's goal is fewer exchanges, not faster ones.

Under Agent-to-Agent RCM, SuperDial takes responsibility for resolving a customer's request across every available channel, so the customer does not have to manage each one. If an electronic transaction can answer the question, SuperDial uses it. If the information sits in a payer portal or can be pulled by faxback, its agents retrieve it there. When a phone call is unavoidable, the agent carries forward what is already known and asks only for what is missing.

The model changes how the value of AI is measured. Most automation vendors count the calls an agent completes, while SuperDial wants to count the work it removes. The platform maintains controls designed to support HIPAA compliance, the US law that protects patient health information. It has also completed a SOC 2 Type II examination, an independent audit of its security controls.

The early data shows what happens when agents talk to agents. Among successful requests where SuperDial retrieved the information it needed, its agents averaged about four minutes per call attempt when the payer used voice automation, against seventeen minutes or more when they reached a human representative.

That makes an AI-to-AI exchange more than four times faster, saving about 13 minutes, or 76%, of each successful attempt. SuperDial says the approach is already helping teams obtain payer information faster with less manual effort. It sees these automated exchanges as an early look at what direct agent-to-agent communication could deliver.

SuperDial was founded by Stanford graduates Sam Schwager, now chief executive, with Harrison Caruthers. The pair previously ran a healthcare billing company and spent thousands of hours on repetitive payer calls. The company began as SuperBill and moved into voice automation in late 2023, then reached seven-figure revenue soon after launch.

It has raised more than $20 million in total, including the $15 million Series A that combined equity with $3 million of venture debt. Its customers include RCM companies and large provider organizations such as dental support organizations and management services organizations.

SuperDial's long-term goal is an AI-native network for payer-provider communication, where agents exchange trusted information directly without repeatedly requesting it across disconnected systems. For payers, that means fewer repetitive inquiries reaching their staff. For providers, it means fewer hours spent chasing information, while patients face fewer administrative delays between them and care.

Ten million calls have shown that AI can take on healthcare's phone burden. SuperDial now wants to power the next billion payer requests through Agent-to-Agent resolution, in a market where McKinsey sees $265 billion a year in savings and where the best call is increasingly the one nobody has to make.

#9636. Reverse proxies and TLS, explained by breaking them

Lots of things broke this week. The server broke lots of times. I expected the causes to be obvious. They were not, and the fastest fixes came from reading what the system was already showing me instead of guessing.

The setup: an Ubuntu VM running nginx in front of two small Python backends, with a firewall and my own certificates. I broke each layer on purpose.

I made one backend slow and expected nginx to hide it. Instead there was no answer, just a very long pause, and then I was given the 504.

nginx accepted the connection and waited for the backend to answer. The backend never did, so after proxy_read_timeout (3 s in my test) nginx gave up. Because timeout is in proxy_next_upstream, it then retried on the second backend and waited again. Two timeouts, 3 s apart, so the 504 arrived after 6 s instead of 3. The error log showed two upstream timed out (110) lines 3 s apart.

To tell them apart, I ignored the exit code and looked at the human-readable error text and the TLS handshake details that curl and OpenSSL print before they give up. Exit code 60 is the problem; the error string and the certificate chain dump are the diagnosis.

The three certificate failures I've seen:

I assumed the firewall rule was the only thing blocking the connection, so removing it should have made curl fail. It still worked.

Forcing each address family told me why: curl -4 timed out (exit 28) and curl -6 worked (exit 0). iptables filters IPv4 only, and I had written no IPv6 rules, so the connection simply went around the firewall. A real host needs ip6tables rules too, and the habit I took from this is to test both address families after any firewall change.

Verify the thing you're about to change is actually the thing in the path: check counters and state before you touch config.

The habit that would have saved the most time: look at the evidence the system is already emitting before forming a theory. iptables -L -v counters, conntrack -L, curl -v, s_client -showcerts — the system was telling me the answer the whole time. I was reading the result (exit code, "still worked") and guessing at the cause instead of reading the mechanism.

What "broken" taught me that working never did: a green checkmark hides which component is actually doing the work. Failure is the only thing that makes the path visible. The long silence, the identical exit code across three different causes — those are the moments the system reveals its real makeup. Working systems let you keep your wrong model forever.

When something surprises you, it's going to be the data. Chase the mechanism, not the outcome: counters, state, and raw output first; theory second.

A founder's most important sales update rarely arrives in a dashboard. It arrives in a message: the champion at a key account has left, a big deal is about to slip a quarter or a call in an hour needs fresh prep. Software has not caught up with that habit. Salespeople still spend only 40% of their time selling, while the rest disappears into research, admin and tools that wait to be opened.

The interface is changing fast. Gartner expects 60% of B2B seller work to run through conversational user interfaces by 2028, up from under 5% in 2023, as sellers move from clicking through dashboards to asking an AI and having it act. More than half of sellers have already used AI agents, while nearly nine in ten plan to by 2027.

Airspeed, the AI-native go-to-market platform founded by former DeepMind researchers, has opened early access to Airbots, an always-on AI chief of staff that lives in WhatsApp and iMessage. Airbots connects to the tools teams already use, spots the deals, calls and follow-ups that need attention and offers to handle them before anyone asks. There is nothing to set up, since it learns how each user and company sells from every reply and correction.

Gartner's forecast marks a shift in how sales software works. Conversational experiences are expected to handle up to 15% of customer meeting prep, 14% of sales planning and 14% of deal negotiation, with the share of seller work running through chat rising roughly twelvefold in five years (our analysis). Gartner also expects a third of chief revenue officers to fund dedicated teams to run generative AI in sales.

The channel matters as much as the model. WhatsApp alone has more than 3 billion monthly users, while founders, investors and salespeople already run much of their working day from their phones. An assistant that sends updates where people already read their messages removes the need to open one more app.

Salesforce's 2026 survey of 4,050 sales professionals found that sellers spend only 40% of their time selling, while 60% goes to research, data entry, admin and internal work (our arithmetic). Sellers expect AI to cut prospect research time by 34% and email drafting time by 36% once it is fully in place, while top performers are 1.7 times more likely than underperformers to use AI agents for prospecting.

More tools have not always meant less work. 51% of sales leaders using AI say disconnected systems slow their projects, so each new bot can add another feed to check. Airspeed's view is that teams need one assistant that sees across the stack, not one bot per job.

Some of the most important signals in sales come from outside the CRM. Lusha's 2026 data found that 12.6% of US sales leaders change roles each year, while 21.7% of UK sales leaders changed roles over twelve months. Its tracking logged about 13,600 company changes every working day in the first half of 2026.

At about 1% a month, a team with 1,000 contacts on active deals should expect around 31 of them to go stale each quarter. When the departing contact is a deal's champion, the internal advocate who pushes the purchase through, the deal can stall quietly unless someone notices the change and finds the replacement in time.

Airbots replaces separate bots for separate jobs with one proactive assistant. Users choose which tools to connect, from Google Workspace to Slack and Salesforce. They then receive tailored text updates about what is happening and when. They can reply to ask a question or hand off a task, just like messaging a colleague.

A typical morning message tells a seller they have five calls that day, warns that their champion at a key account left last week, says Airbots has already found her replacement and offers to draft an introduction before 2pm. Behind each message sits a team of agents that keeps working across email, CRM and connected tools without waiting to be asked.

Airbots learns as it goes. It needs no configuration, since it picks up each user's selling style and their company's playbook from every reply and correction until it works like a second version of the user. The more tools it can see, the more it can do, from spotting a lost Salesforce deal worth reopening to checking that every large deal sits in the right forecast category across HubSpot and Gong.

Users always stay in control. Airbots never sends an email unless a user asks it to, while users choose which tools it can access and can disconnect any of them at any time. Airspeed is SOC 2 Type II compliant, an independent standard for how a company protects customer data.

For sales reps, Airbots points out when the deals they are focused on will not get them to quota, finds a new stakeholder to re-engage stalled deals and spots accounts they have not touched this quarter, with a reason to reach out and a draft ready to send. Sales leaders see where the quarter is likely to land and which deals could slip, while founders can set their priorities for the week and let Airbots keep them on track as new requests come in.

The assistant reaches beyond the sales team. Marketers can ask whether a campaign is coming up on sales calls, while post-sale teams can get suggested next actions, look up what a customer pays straight from the contract, catch hanging threads and refresh call prep at the last minute. When a contract champion leaves, Airbots can flag it immediately and find the new contact on LinkedIn.

Airspeed was founded in 2022 by chief executive Adam Liska and chief technology officer Devang Agrawal, who left Google DeepMind together to start the company in London. Liska holds a PhD in brain and cognitive sciences and previously worked at Spotify and Facebook, while Agrawal studied engineering at Cambridge.

Airspeed describes itself as the execution layer for revenue teams, turning what is said in calls, emails and meetings into the next action that moves a deal forward, from CRM updates to deal risk to coaching. It serves more than 180 customers in 20 countries, including Persona, Qdrant and Pricefx. The company is headquartered in London and New York.

The company raised a $20 million Series A in June 2026 led by DN Capital, taking total funding past $25 million. Its investors include Framework Venture Partners, Vi Partners, Atlassian Ventures, Point72 Ventures and Creator Fund.

Growth has been strong. Airspeed's revenue grew fourfold year on year at the time of its Series A, while customers built thousands of custom agents in the first four months of 2026 and monthly agent runs nearly tripled between January and April. Airbots extends that platform from the desktop into the place many users spend most of their day, their messaging apps.

Airbots is available in early access, with a waitlist open at Airbots.ai. Founders, investors and sales teams can join to connect their tools and start receiving updates in WhatsApp or iMessage.

The direction of sales software is clear. Gartner expects most seller work to run through conversation within a few years, while sellers are adopting AI agents faster than their tools can coordinate them. Airspeed is building one proactive assistant that knows the whole pipeline and speaks up first, giving every seller and founder a chief of staff that lives where they already work.

#9633. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9632. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. #9631. eBPF Tutorial by Example 11: Develop User-Space Programs with libbpf and Trace exec() and exit()

eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a powerful network and performance analysis tool on the Linux kernel. It allows developers to dynamically load, update, and run user-defined code during kernel runtime.

In this tutorial, we will learn how kernel-space and user-space eBPF programs work together. We will also learn how to use the native libbpf to develop user-space programs, package eBPF applications into executable files, and distribute them across different kernel versions.

The complete source code: https://github.com/eunomia-bpf/bpf-developer-tutorial/tree/main/src/11-bootstrap

libbpf is a C language library that is distributed with the kernel version to assist in loading and running eBPF programs. It provides a set of C APIs for interacting with the eBPF system, allowing developers to write user-space programs more easily to load and manage eBPF programs. These user-space programs are typically used for system performance analysis, monitoring, or optimization.

There are several advantages to using the libbpf library:

At the same time, libbpf and BTF (BPF Type Format) are important components of the eBPF ecosystem. They play critical roles in achieving compatibility across different kernel versions. BTF is a metadata format used to describe type information in eBPF programs. The primary purpose of BTF is to provide a structured way to describe data structures in the kernel so that eBPF programs can access and manipulate them more easily.

The key roles of BTF in achieving compatibility across different kernel versions are as follows:

By combining libbpf and BTF, eBPF programs can run on various kernel versions without the need for separate compilation for each kernel version. This greatly improves the portability and compatibility of the eBPF ecosystem and reduces the difficulty of development and maintenance.

Bootstrap is a complete application that utilizes libbpf. It uses eBPF programs to trace the exec() system call in the kernel (handled by the SEC("tp/sched/sched_process_exec") handle_exec BPF program), which mainly corresponds to the creation of new processes (excluding the fork() part). In addition, it also traces the exit() system call of processes (handled by the SEC("tp/sched/sched_process_exit") handle_exit BPF program) to understand when each process exits.

These two BPF programs work together to capture interesting information about new processes, such as the file name of the binary and measure the lifecycle of processes. They also collect interesting statistics, such as exit codes or resource consumption, when a process exits. This is a good starting point to gain a deeper understanding of the inner workings of the kernel and observe how things actually operate.

Bootstrap also uses the argp API (part of libc) for command-line argument parsing, allowing users to configure the behavior of the application through command-line options. This provides flexibility and allows users to customize the program behavior according to their specific needs. While these functionalities can also be achieved using the eunomia-bpf tool, using libbpf here provides higher scalability in user space at the cost of additional complexity.

Bootstrap consists of two parts: kernel space and user space. The kernel space part is an eBPF program that traces the exec() and exit() system calls. The user space part is a C language program that uses the libbpf library to load and run the kernel space program and process the data collected from the kernel space program.

This code is a kernel-level eBPF program (bootstrap.bpf.c) used to trace exec() and exit() system calls. It captures process creation and exit events using an eBPF program and sends the relevant information to a user-space program for processing. Below is a detailed explanation of the code.

First, we include the necessary headers and define the license for the eBPF program. We also define two eBPF maps: exec_start and rb. exec_start is a hash type eBPF map used to store the timestamp when a process starts executing. rb is a ring buffer type eBPF map used to store captured event data and send it to the user-space program.

Next, we define an eBPF program named handle_exec which is triggered when a process executes the exec() system call. First, we retrieve the PID from the current process, record the timestamp when the process starts executing, and store it in the exec_start map.

Then, we reserve an event structure from the circular buffer map rb and fill in the relevant data, such as the process ID, parent process ID, and process name. Afterwards, we send this data to the user-mode program for processing.

Finally, we define an eBPF program named handle_exit that will be triggered when a process executes the exit() system call. First, we retrieve the PID and TID (thread ID) from the current process. If the PID and TID are not equal, it means that this is a thread exit, and we will ignore this event.

Next, we look up the timestamp of when the process started execution, which was previously stored in the exec_start map. If a timestamp is found, we calculate the process's lifetime duration and then remove the record from the exec_start map. If a timestamp is not found and a minimum duration is specified, we return directly.

Then, we reserve an event structure from the circular buffer map rb and fill in the relevant data, such as the process ID, parent process ID, process name, and process duration. Finally, we send this data to the user-mode program for processing.

This way, when a process executes the exec() or exit() system calls, our eBPF program captures the corresponding events and sends detailed information to the user space program for further processing. This allows us to easily monitor process creation and termination and obtain detailed information about the processes.

In addition, in the bootstrap.h file, we also define the data structures for interaction with user space:

First, we define an env structure to store command line arguments:

Next, we use the argp library to parse command line arguments:

In the main() function, we first parse the command line arguments, and then set the libbpf print callback function libbpf_print_fn to output debug information when needed:

Next, we open the eBPF skeleton file, pass the minimum duration parameter to the eBPF program, and load and attach the eBPF program:

Then, we create a ring buffer to receive event data sent by the eBPF program:

The handle_event() function handles events received from the eBPF program. Depending on the event type (process execution or exit), it extracts and prints event information such as timestamp, process name, process ID, parent process ID, file name, or exit code.

Finally, we use the ring_buffer__poll() function to poll the ring buffer and process the received event data:

Through this example, we have learned how to combine eBPF programs with user-space programs. This combination provides developers with a powerful toolkit for efficient data collection and processing across the kernel and user space. By using eBPF and libbpf, you can build more efficient, scalable, and secure monitoring and performance analysis tools.

In the following tutorials, we will continue to explore the advanced features of eBPF and share more about eBPF development practices. Through continuous learning and practice, you will have a better understanding and mastery of eBPF technology and apply it to solve real-world problems.

#9630. Motorcycle Helmets Are Becoming Giant Airbags. Could Helmets that Inflate like Airbags Work?

Silently sculpting systems and synchronizing synchronous harmony, breathing life into machines.

Silently sculpting systems and synchronizing synchronous harmony, breathing life into machines.

Silently sculpting systems and synchronizing synchronous harmony, breathing life into machines.

Imagine riding a motorcycle when a car pulls out in front of you. Before your head strikes the road, your helmet expands into an enormous protective cushion. That is the promise behind an emerging category of airbag-equipped head protection.

The latest attention centers on Chinese manufacturer Lanxi Yema Motorcycle Fittings, described in November 17 reporting. But Italian helmet maker Airoh and Swedish safety supplier Autoliv unveiled a related prototype in 2022. Sweden’s Hövding sold inflatable bicycle head protectors for years before going bankrupt, while Britain’s Ventete sells a helmet inflated before use.

Lanxi Yema Motorcycle Fittings is an established helmet manufacturer in Zhejiang, China. Its website claims a large factory and substantial conventional helmet production capacity. Those figures should not be mistaken for sales of its airbag design.

A Chinese utility model, CN224761381U: A Helmet Airbag Arrangement, was published September 18, 2026, following a November 2025 application. The patent supports the existence of a development project, not commercial availability or independently demonstrated protection.

The concept adds inflatable protection to a conventional helmet. A sensor and triggering system would need to detect a crash, activate an inflator and expand cushioning before head impact. I could not verify retail availability, a price, independently certified testing, an original manufacturer demonstration video or sales figures for this specific product.

At the 2022 EICMA motorcycle show, Airoh and Autoliv unveiled what their official announcement called a helmet concept with an integrated airbag. The airbag was designed to deploy around the crown of a conventional helmet, retaining the underlying helmet as protection even without deployment.

The British Motorcyclists Federation’s description explains how shell sections open to allow inflation. Autoliv’s technical brochure described preliminary impact research and estimated that, under modeled conditions, a serious skull-fracture injury probability could fall from about 60% to 30%. This is not a demonstrated halving of motorcycle deaths or a universal crash-risk estimate.

The project drew on earlier academic research, including work associated with Sheffield Hallam University. Yet I could not verify a commercial launch or unit sales for the integrated helmet. Autoliv remains active in motorcycle airbags: its 2026 partnership with RS Taichi concerns an airbag vest, and Cycle World reported on a motorcycle-mounted system intended to protect the rider’s upper body and head. Neither is proof the integrated helmet has shipped.

Hövding’s device was a collar worn by cyclists. Motion sensors attempted to identify a crash, triggering an inflatable hood around the head. The company described inflation in approximately 0.1 seconds and substantial development involving staged accidents. Its documentary announcement discusses the testing process; watch the documentary.

Unlike the motorcycle prototypes, this product reached a sizable market. A 2022 research publication from Germany’s Institute for Motorcycle Safety reported approximately 425,000 units sold since 2013. That is a historical count, not a confirmed lifetime total.

In 2023 Swedish authorities questioned the reliability of Hövding 3, imposed sales restrictions and initiated a recall. The company contested the action, but filed for bankruptcy in December 2023. Bikerumor’s account describes the legal and commercial fallout. A successful inflation demonstration did not settle questions about real-world reliability.

Austria’s iSi Group subsequently acquired the technology and intellectual property, according to the bankruptcy administrator. The Hövding website describes a forthcoming Hövding 4 with redesigned electronics and crash-detection software. It is intended for cycling, not motorcycling, and I could not verify a firm launch date or preorder availability.

British startup Ventete takes a simpler approach: inflate the helmet before riding, then deflate it for storage. Its aH-1 uses interconnected inflatable structures rather than a crash-triggered gas generator. A Financial Times profile reported years of development and an initial release that sold out quickly, without establishing cumulative sales.

The official product page lists versions priced at £185, £200 and £225, depending on the pump. Ventete’s FAQ explicitly says the helmet is not for motorcycles or mopeds. Its official video links include an inflation demonstration.

This distinction is essential: a pre-inflated bicycle helmet does not need to recognize an imminent crash. It instead must reliably maintain pressure, resist damage and protect the rider across relevant impact conditions.

Bumpair is another project focused on inflatable, compact bicycle head protection. An engineering case study describes work on skull fit, pressure retention and manufacturing, as well as a 2022 road-safety innovation prize. I could not verify large-scale sales or a certified motorcycle-specific version.

The underlying physics are plausible. Increasing the distance and time over which a head decelerates can reduce peak impact acceleration. But that does not automatically translate into lower brain-injury risk in every crash. Deployment timing, rotational forces, neck loading, and the behavior of the helmet without inflation all matter.

At 60 mph, a motorcycle travels about 2.7 meters in 100 milliseconds. A system that needs that long to inflate must detect danger early enough to finish deployment before the relevant head impact. An algorithm that misses a crash may provide no additional airbag protection; one that deploys unnecessarily introduces different risks.

Crash types also vary: direct impacts, glancing blows, sliding, tumbling and collisions with obstacles are not interchangeable. A peer-reviewed study of motorcycle helmets under oblique impacts emphasizes the importance of rotational injury measurements and impact location. A larger protective surface is not necessarily safer in every configuration.

The neck matters too. A 2023 biomechanics study involving airbag and helmet protection explored reductions in certain impact measures alongside potential neck-loading tradeoffs. It would be premature to generalize its results to all inflatable helmet designs.

Certification is another hurdle. A crash-triggered motorcycle helmet should be evaluated for ordinary helmet protection, successful deployment and failures to deploy. The Bicycle Helmet Safety Institute’s analysis of airbag headgear explains the regulatory complications faced by unconventional bicycle protection. Motorcycle approval requires its own applicable standards and testing.

Motorcycle-mounted airbags and wearable airbag vests already exist. Honda introduced an airbag-equipped Gold Wing in 2006, and suppliers have developed tethered and electronically triggered wearable systems. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety discusses motorcycle airbag approaches and the limits of available real-world effectiveness evidence.

But a vest protecting the torso does not validate an inflatable structure around the head. Head injury biomechanics and crash timing create different requirements.

For Yema, the meaningful next milestones are independently published impact data, an applicable certification, an official demonstration with measured deployment timing, and confirmed customer deliveries. For Airoh and Autoliv, the unanswered question is whether the integrated helmet concept will become a retail product. For Hövding, the test is whether its new ownership can relaunch with dependable crash detection and regulatory acceptance.

The industry needs comparable testing across impact speeds, angles, surfaces and accident sequences, including linear and rotational acceleration, neck loading, and deployment failures. A slow-motion promotional video cannot substitute for those results.

Airbag helmets challenge the assumption that head protection must stay the same shape throughout a ride. Inflatable structures could add impact-management space only when needed. The concept is credible, and several companies have invested real engineering effort in it.

Yet the strongest evidence is still fragmented: a Chinese patent, a European prototype with promising modeled results, a once-successful bicycle product that collapsed amid regulatory concerns, and a commercial bicycle helmet inflated before use. None of that establishes that an integrated crash-triggered motorcycle airbag helmet has achieved proven, mass-market protection.

The future may involve helmets that transform in a crash. Until independent testing and certification support a particular product, riders should rely on appropriately certified conventional motorcycle helmets rather than an experimental airbag promise.

#9629. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9625. AI Agents Turn Egress Into a Security Boundary

Principal Product Manager working on Cloud Networking and Network security.

Principal Product Manager working on Cloud Networking and Network security.

Principal Product Manager working on Cloud Networking and Network security.

This follows an earlier piece I wrote on how AI agents slip past existing controls[i]. That article asked whether your network and resources can even tell an agent apart from a human or a service, and what controls they need against an agent's non-deterministic actions. Nearly every question I got back landed on two things: how does an agent make data exfiltration risk worse, and what does an optimal egress control look like. So, this piece focuses solely on egress.

An AI agent is an outbound machine. It takes a task, reasons about it, then reaches out: to a model API, a vector store, a SaaS tool, a Model Context Protocol server, another team's agent, often an endpoint on the public internet. One request can fan out into dozens of calls the agent chose on its own, based on text it was reasoning over. Your network was not built for a caller that picks its own destinations at runtime.

In many environments there is little egress control, because outbound was never where the perceived risk lived. Ingress got the web application firewalls, the rate limits, the scrutiny. Outbound came from software the team wrote, so it was trusted by default and allowed to leave.

The controls that do exist are rarely thorough: a firewall sits on one path while a second gateway, a peered network, a managed service endpoint, or a developer's convenience route stays uninspected. It looks governed on a diagram and is porous in practice. That is what an agent lands in: not a tight allowlist it must subvert, but a broad outbound path that is often patchily filtered.

For teams that have done the work, outbound policy rests on one assumption: the workload is predictable. A service talks to a known set of dependencies. You enumerate IP ranges, ports and domain names, deny the rest, and it holds, because the software does the same thing every run. That was sound until agents arrived.

Agents break that assumption. An agent picks which tool or model to call based on reasoning shaped by inputs you do not control, so the endpoints it might reach are not known when you write the policy. A static list ends up too tight, and the agent fails, or too loose, and it becomes a general-purpose outbound channel. Making the list longer does not resolve that.

Two problems compound this. Sensitive data usually rides inside ordinary application content, so exfiltration looks like a well-formed API call to a legitimate domain, the damage sitting in the words rather than the connection. And agent-to-agent and agent-to-tool calls create lateral traffic between workloads that previously had no reason to talk, extending a compromised agent's reach.

The most consequential agent attacks disclosed so far are, at their core, egress attacks. The attacker never breaks in. They get a trusted agent to send data out.

When Legit Security disclosed CamoLeak in GitHub Copilot Chat in October 2025, hidden instructions in a repository persuaded the assistant to push private source code and secrets out through a channel the network permitted[ii]. When Zenity Labs demonstrated AgentFlayer at Black Hat USA 2025, one poisoned document made enterprise assistants rummage through connected systems and hand credentials back out[iii]. In both cases the credential was valid and the destination reachable. What was missing was not authentication but any governance of where the agent's traffic could go and what it could carry.

The first move is not policy authoring. It is inventory. You cannot inspect traffic leaving through a door you have not found, and there are usually more doors than anyone believes.

Enumerate every path traffic can leave by: internet and egress gateways, proxies, peered and transit connections into porous networks, VPN tunnels, managed-service endpoints, DNS paths and any developer-provisioned shortcut added for convenience and never removed. Then reduce that set deliberately onto a small number of controlled exits. Every path you remove is one less to monitor.

This matters more with agents than with conventional workloads. Paths proliferate as workloads multiply, and at scale inspecting every route individually stops being feasible. A compromised agent with excess privileges can influence routing, try alternate paths, and reach an exit nobody thought to cover. If one uninspected route exists, assume the agent finds it. The objective is structural: find every exit, minimize them, inspect what remains, so nothing leaves without passing a control.

With the exits consolidated and inspected, the next control is what they permit. The baseline is default-deny: nothing leaves unless a rule explicitly allows it. That inverts the burden of proof. Instead of enumerating what is forbidden, an unbounded and losing exercise, you enumerate what is permitted; everything else fails by construction.

Default-deny only pays off when the allowlist is source-based. One global list applied uniformly at an exit means every workload behind it inherits the union of everyone's permissions, and a single compromised workload's blast radius becomes the entire allowlist. A source-based rule binds a specific source to specific destinations, so what one workload may reach does not open that destination for its neighbor.

Enforcing that list does not require reading traffic. The destination hostname is usually visible in the TLS handshake before the session is encrypted, and resolvers are a control point in their own right, since an agent cannot connect to a name they refuse to answer. Both have limits. Encrypted Client Hello conceals that hostname, so policy needs an IP and reputation fallback[iv]. And DNS controls nothing unless you also block outbound DoH and DoT, or the agent resolves elsewhere; that exact bypass has already defeated a CI egress allowlist[v]. Enforcement location matters more than any single observable.

Destination lists alone leave the hardest question unanswered: which agent is this. The policy you want is not "can this host reach that address," but "may this specific agent, owned by this team, acting for this user, reach this destination."

That requires the agent's identity and provenance to travel with the request to the egress boundary, the recognition problem the first article argued must be solved first. Provenance is the precondition for policy. Without it, every agent behind a shared exit is indistinguishable and source-based rules collapse into one network-wide list.

The model to aim for is an agent that starts with no outbound reach at all, with every destination it needs declared, reviewed and granted in its own definition alongside its identity and owner, not retrofitted into a firewall rule afterwards. A new endpoint later is a change to approve, not a runtime decision it makes for itself.

Denials must be explicit and legible: a refused call should return a structured rejection the agent can reason about and fall back from, because a denial that looks like a timeout invites retries and probing, exactly what you do not want from a system that improvises. And deny-by-default holds when the agent is hijacked, because the boundary never consults the agent's judgment about where it may go. That is why this belongs at the network, not inside the agent.

Destination policy governs where traffic goes. It cannot tell you what that traffic carries, and since sensitive data rides inside ordinary application content, that gap is where exfiltration happens. The temptation is to intercept TLS everywhere. That is the wrong answer. Plenty of destinations will not accept an intermediate proxy's certificate and simply break, decrypting at volume is expensive, and terminating all TLS gives the firewall plaintext access to everything, a fresh high-value target with new compliance obligations. Done indiscriminately, it solves a visibility problem by manufacturing a custody problem.

The opposite extreme is wrong too. Ideally you would permit only known, trusted destinations. But when enterprises open a path for general workforce or workload traffic, they usually deploy the inverse: allow everything except what is already known to be malicious. Traffic then splits into two populations treated identically: destinations you have vetted, and destinations whose posture is unknown. A steerable agent will happily use the second. Bounded agents avoid this through the source-based allowlist, but some legitimately need broad reach, browsing or calling third-party APIs chosen at runtime, so the unknown population is unavoidable.

So tier the control by destination trust. For trusted, vetted destinations, do not decrypt; you already know the endpoint. For unknown or uncategorized ones, decrypt selectively: outbound, run data-leak prevention so sensitive content cannot reach an endpoint nobody has evaluated; inbound, scan what returns, because content from an unvetted source is where malware and poisoned instructions enter, and an agent that ingests it will act on it. That confines cost and breakage to the traffic that warrants scrutiny and concentrates inspection where your knowledge is weakest.

Everything so far concerns traffic leaving your environment. The east-west direction, agents calling other agents and tools, needs the same discipline applied to internal reach, where least privilege does the work. That is what checks lateral movement by a compromised agent.

An agent should reach only the internal endpoints its task requires. A customer-support agent has no business reaching a code repository, and a build agent has no business reaching a payments API. Scope each agent to what its job demands, express that once in its definition, and enforce it at the boundary rather than trusting the agent to behave. On a flat internal network the opposite holds by default: any agent reaches almost anything, so one hijacked agent inherits the whole environment's reach.

Treat these calls as trust-boundary crossings, not free movement: mutual authentication, inspection out and back, and segmentation so the internal endpoints an agent can reach are as deliberately chosen as the external ones. The return path matters as much as the request: a response from a compromised agent or tool is another way poisoned instructions arrive. The protocol layer is young too: the default MCP transport shipped at the end of 2024 with insufficient authentication, so do not assume these hops are safe[vi].

Finally, make the traffic answerable. Every outbound flow should be attributable to a specific agent, its owner, and the human it acted for, and queryable afterward. "Which external destinations did any agent reach this month, and which agent reached them" should be one question with one answer at the boundary, not a forensics exercise after something has gone wrong. Where you do inspect payloads, pair the flow record with what was sent.

Knowing an agent is an agent is necessary but inert on its own. That knowledge becomes an enforceable limit on the outbound path, the last point where a decision can be made that the agent cannot override. Corrupt the model, poison its inputs, talk it into a plan no designer imagined, and the data still has to leave through an exit you control, provided there is no other way out.

The agents are already calling out. The work is making sure something is deciding, on your behalf, which of those calls should ever leave the environment.

This article was published under HackerNoon's Business Blogging program.

[i] HackerNoon, The Impostor in Your Environment Is the AI Agent Holding a Valid Credential.

[ii] Legit Security, CamoLeak: Critical GitHub Copilot Vulnerability Leaks Private Source Code.

[iii] Zenity Labs via PR Newswire, Zenity Labs Exposes Widespread “AgentFlayer” Vulnerabilities Allowing Silent Hijacking of Major Enterprise AI Agents Circumventing Human Oversight.

[iv] Cisco, Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) Defense Strategies: How Cisco Secure Firewall Tackles ECH.

[v] GitHub Advisory Database, Egress Policy Bypass via DNS over HTTPS (DoH) in Harden-Runner (Community Tier).

[vi] Vectara, MCP’s Rapid Journey: From Open Door to a Fortified Gateway

The Egress Security Your Environment Needs For Safe Agent Conduct
