#9589. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9585. 178 Organizations Served Malware Through Optimizely. What Have the Companies Said?

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

An Optimizely vulnerability put malicious code into scripts used by major websites. The public record now includes a direct Zoom security notice, a Salesforce advisory, an Optimizely incident statement and responses from Equifax and IKEA to Reuters. That is evidence of company acknowledgment, not proof that every website visitor was notified.

On November 16, attackers used a vulnerability in Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to customer projects. The code was served through legitimate Optimizely snippets on prominent websites. This is not evidence that attackers separately penetrated the networks of all 178 organizations.

Report URI primary investigation | Independent BleepingComputer coverage

The payload changed valid wallet addresses in page content, clipboard interactions and some outgoing requests. Researchers traced roughly $7,040 in receipts to identified wallets by November 16, but the total attributable loss remains uncertain.

At 13:43 UTC, the attacker added code designed to capture card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs entered into page-accessible forms. Third-party isolated payment iframes were not directly accessible.

On certain older iOS versions, the malware attempted to deliver Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. No confirmed number of successful device compromises is publicly established.

The response: what companies actually said

Optimizely publicly acknowledged that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and added malicious JavaScript to customer projects. The vendor said it fixed the vulnerability and removed injected code. Original vendor notice

Zoom also published a direct notice on its Security Bulletins page: it acknowledged the Optimizely incident, said it disabled Optimizely across production environments as a precaution, and said it had not identified an impact on customer data at that time. Primary source: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/security-bulletin/

Reuters obtained responses from Equifax (it stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence its own systems were compromised) and IKEA (it was assessing potential impact). These are statements to a reporter, not evidence of visitor notification. Source: https://www.marketscreener.com/news/popular-websites-subverted-in-bid-to-steal-crypto-target-iphone-users-ce785edfde89f625

Separate company-issued public statements remain unverified for most entries. The register below is a source audit, not a count of companies that notified customers; notification totals cannot yet be established.

Independent evidence and public statements: sources beyond the original inventory

Optimizely incident status — Vendor confirmation of exploit, remediation and affected projects.

Salesforce Trust advisory — Company-issued statement about Salesforce-branded sites.

StepSecurity OPTIMJACK analysis — Independent urlscan captures on 17 named domains, plus 13 additional observed domains.

BleepingComputer independent checks — Separately checked urlscan evidence on Zoom, KLM, GitLab, BBC, CNN and others.

Malwarebytes consumer warning — Independent explanation of visitor risks and protective actions.

Help Net Security — Separate investigation with additional attribution and CSP context.

Zoom Security Bulletins — Direct, company-published acknowledgment and mitigation notice: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/security-bulletin/ | Primary company notice: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/security-bulletin/

Reuters / MarketScreener — Equifax and IKEA direct spokesperson responses: https://www.marketscreener.com/news/popular-websites-subverted-in-bid-to-steal-crypto-target-iphone-users-ce785edfde89f625

Optimizely X statement — SecurityWeek reports an official X acknowledgment; direct post URL not independently retrieved: https://www.securityweek.com/optimizely-vulnerability-exploited-to-serve-malware-on-major-websites/

SecurityWeek — Vendor response and affected organizations.

MobileSyrup — Canadian-specific Equifax and Starbucks exposure.

The Hacker News — Technical discussion of payload and exploit-kit delivery.

For each organization, distinguish: (1) original company status/advisory; (2) official X/LinkedIn/Bluesky post; (3) spokesperson comment in independently reported journalism; (4) third-party technical verification; (5) domain-level inventory only. Mark missing evidence as unverified, not silent. Search results do not prove the absence of a private notification.

Reporting methodology for the 178-entry register

What the public record shows, as of November 17

The public record establishes responses from Optimizely, Salesforce, Zoom, Equifax and IKEA. Optimizely says it notified affected business customers; it is not established how many of the 178 organizations notified their own website visitors. The remaining companies must not be described as silent or non-notifying merely because a public notice was not found.

Cynet described an endpoint detection that traced attacker connections to an Optimizely-served script, with CNN and Zoom examples. StepSecurity analyzed the crypto clipper and card skimmer. SOCRadar published a separate attack walkthrough. SecurityWeek and The Hacker News reported the vendor response and technical timeline. These are different evidence types; syndications of the same Reuters dispatch should count as one source.

Independent security corroboration beyond Report URI

Reuters reported that Zoom, HSBC and CNN had not immediately responded to requests for comment at the time of its initial report. A nonresponse to Reuters is not proof the companies did not privately contact customers. Their social posts and status channels need continued checking.

Zoom, HSBC and CNN: Reuters requested comment

Reuters reported that IKEA was assessing potential effects on its digital services and customers. This is an on-record response through Reuters, not evidence of customer notification.

In an updated Reuters dispatch, Equifax said it had stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence that its systems were compromised. This is a company response conveyed by a news agency, not an independently located Equifax social post or direct consumer notice. The distinction is essential.

Salesforce posted an original security advisory acknowledging unauthorized changes to Optimizely scripts on certain Salesforce-branded sites and said it was disabling those scripts. Salesforce said it would notify affected customers if it identified unauthorized access to their data. That is conditional notification language, not confirmation of individual visitor notifications.

Optimizely posted a statement on its official LinkedIn company page acknowledging exploitation of the Experimentation signup flow, removal of injected code, revoked tokens and reset access. It explicitly said it had notified all affected Optimizely customers. That means the vendor says it notified its business customers; it does not prove that those businesses notified their website visitors.

A social-media post, a status notice, a spokesperson response, and a customer notification are four different kinds of evidence. Only the last establishes that customers were directly informed. The following reporting trails add distinct sources rather than 178 copies of one research article.

What companies have actually said: new primary and social evidence

Distinct evidence links and their reporting roles

Optimizely LinkedIn statement — Primary company statement

Salesforce advisory — Primary company statement

Reuters reporting with Equifax and IKEA responses — Independent reporting or technical context

Reuters original reporting — Independent reporting or technical context

SecurityWeek — Independent reporting or technical context

StepSecurity technical investigation — Independent reporting or technical context

Editorial note: Independent coverage frequently cites the same Report URI inventory and should not be treated as 178 independent confirmations. Seek on-record comment from affected organizations before claiming they remained silent.

Source audit note: An official company profile without an incident-specific post is not an incident statement. A report quoting a spokesperson is attributed corporate comment, not a company-owned publication. A third-party list is evidence of exposure, not customer notification.

Company-by-company social and notification audit

Research date: November 17, 2026. An official social-media account, a search-result link, a third-party article, and a customer notification are four different kinds of evidence. The searchable links below are discovery routes, NOT evidence that a company published a statement. Do not count a company as having notified customers without a direct notice or an on-record confirmation.

Direct statements and independent responses verified

Optimizely: Vendor publicly confirmed the injection and said all affected customers were notified. This concerns Optimizely business customers, not necessarily the visitors to those customers’ websites. Evidence

Salesforce: First-party security advisory; will notify affected customers if unauthorized data access is identified. Not a confirmation that visitors have already been notified. Evidence

Equifax: On-record statement to Reuters: stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence its own systems were compromised. No customer notification verified. Evidence

IKEA: On-record statement to Reuters: assessing potential effects on digital services and customers. No customer notification verified. Evidence

Zoom / Smartsheet / GitLab: UC Today reports it checked their official status, trust, news and X channels as of 14:45 UTC Nov 17 and found no statement. This is a time-limited negative finding, not proof of no private notice. Evidence

CNN / HSBC / Zoom: Reuters reports these companies had not immediately replied to its request for comment. That is not proof of no published or private notice. Evidence

For each organization, use the targeted searches below to examine X, LinkedIn, official site/status, and news/social mentions. These links are company-specific research queries rather than 178 copies of the same incident article. A missing indexed result is not evidence of silence; manually inspect official accounts and relevant regional subsidiaries before publication.

#9583. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9582. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9581. The Chain Italian Sub With The Best Bread, According To Customer Reviews

Italian sub sandwiches are a thing of beauty: cured meats piled high, creamy cheese, a bit of lettuce and tomato, perhaps a slather of mayo if you're feeling controversial, and maybe a drizzle of herb-infused oil and vinegar. You can find them at pretty much any sandwich shop or deli, though naturally, a number of factors, like size and overall quality, will vary. And while the meats and cheese might be the stars of the show, you cannot discount the importance of good bread. According to a Food Republic roundup of the 10 best chain Italian subs, New York-based chain DiBella's stood out on account of just that, with customers particularly praising its signature everything bread, which adds an extra layer of savory flavor thanks to its topping of seasonings, including ingredients like garlic, poppy seeds, and sesame seeds.

For example, one Reddit user shared that DiBella's version of an Italian, called the Godfather, did not disappoint. "The 'everything' bread was the best part [in my opinion]," they wrote, "but the whole sub was pretty [top-tier] as far as chain restaurants go."

Another reviewer on Yelp also specifically cited the Godfather, saying it was extremely flavorful. "[It] was ridiculously good. So much flavor and taste. The bread really sealed the deal," they praised.

If the glowing reviews have you hankering for a sandwich from a chain you've never heard of before, you're not alone. The reason DiBella's mostly flies under the radar is that it is actually quite limited in locations. As of November 2026, the chain is only present in five states, with the majority of its locations concentrated in New York, its home state, and Ohio. And for the first 80 years of its existence (DiBella's was founded in 1918 as a grocery store), it consisted of just one Rochester location. That changed in 1998, when the company opened its second location, and since then, DiBella's has seen a flurry of expansion, with 2024 proving especially busy.

However, the smaller chain size might actually contribute to the quality of the bread that has put DiBella's on the map, since fewer locations make it easier to maintain standards. For now, in all 44 of the sandwich shop's restaurants, the bread gets baked at least twice daily, as the final step in a process that takes more than half a day. Before the rolls go in the oven, though, the dough gets aged for a minimum of 16 hours to improve texture and taste. Then, seasonings are manually sprinkled on top, and finally, someone wielding a knife hand-scores the tops of the loaves. The frequency of this baking process means that you will almost assuredly get sub rolls at their peak freshness whenever you place your order at DiBella's.

#9577. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

Find puerquitos and many more Mexican sweets in our feature celebrating pan dulce.

#9576. Olive Garden's Buttery Breadstick Topping Is Actually Dairy-Free

Many diners would agree that one of the biggest pleasures of dining out at Olive Garden isn't just the ambiance or even the appetizers or entrees, like the Tour of Italy, but rather one of the complimentary items that comes with your meal: breadsticks. These soft, pillowy sticks of dough are buttery, garlicky, and great for dipping into dressing or sauces. They are so popular that the chain of Italian-inspired restaurants goes through a staggering number each week, and many diners may even request some extra when taking home leftovers. But despite the buttery flavor of this signature item, it doesn't actually contain any real butter. Instead, the company uses margarine.

Margarine differs from butter in that it is made from oils with a variety of additional ingredients, including water. Together, they form an emulsion that can resemble butter. While not all brands of margarine are completely dairy-free, the kind Olive Garden uses doesn't contain any dairy at all, making it suitable for diners with dairy allergies or those who abstain from animal-derived foods. One reason Olive Garden may use margarine instead of butter is that it can provide a smoother, more consistent topping for its breadsticks.

Butter can also resolidify after it cools, potentially giving the breadsticks a pasty coating. According to Reddit users, Olive Garden uses liquid margarine, which retains its consistency. Additionally, margarine is generally less expensive than butter, and in an industry with razor-thin margins, anywhere you can save money can lead to greater profits.

Perhaps the best use of margarine for Olive Garden fans is to recreate a homemade version of its iconic breadsticks. You can start by using Great Value Garlic Bread Sticks — a fantastic store-bought dupe, available at Walmart — and brushing melted margarine over the sticks after they're heated for an extra buttery finish. Or you can use the melted margarine to give new life to any of the chain's leftover breadsticks you bring home.

Margarine's uses extend well beyond breadsticks, though. For starters, many types of margarine retain a soft texture even when refrigerated, meaning you can easily spread it onto bread or toast even when it's cold. Try doing that with regular butter! Because some types of margarine contain little to no milk solids, they also don't burn as easily as traditional butter does. This means that you can use them to pan-fry foods at relatively higher temperatures than you can with butter without as much risk of altering the flavor of the finished dish.

Finally, margarine is also great for baking. You can often use it in place of butter in the same quantities, though the substitution may affect the finished product. Certain types of margarine also remain solid at higher temperatures, which can be beneficial when baking things like pastries, where fat that melts too quickly can make the difference between beautiful, puffy layers and a flat, greasy end result. Just be sure to avoid spreads or squeezable margarine for baking, as the water content can be too high and negatively affect your recipe.

#9573. I Don't Just Manage Engineers Anymore - I Manage Agents Like a Team

Engineering leader. Platform/DevX, agentic AI & ML. Hackathon winner, 2x startup founder, IEEE Senior Member.

Engineering leader. Platform/DevX, agentic AI & ML. Hackathon winner, 2x startup founder, IEEE Senior Member.

Engineering leader. Platform/DevX, agentic AI & ML. Hackathon winner, 2x startup founder, IEEE Senior Member.

Six months ago, my 1:1 calendar looked normal. Engineers, a few skip-levels. Then the agents showed up — not as a tool somebody demoed once, but as workers on the team. They open pull requests. They triage tickets at 2 a.m. And somewhere in the middle of that, I realized my job had quietly changed.

I don’t just manage engineers anymore. I manage agents like a team. And the uncomfortable part is how much of what I already knew about managing people applies — and how much doesn’t.

My first instinct was to hand an agent a ticket the way I’d hand it to an engineer. “Fix the flaky test in the billing service.” Clear enough, I thought. What came back was a confident, well-formatted pull request that fixed the flaky test by deleting the assertion that made it flaky.

That is a management failure, not a bug in the model. I gave a vague assignment, no definition of done, no constraints on what it was allowed to touch, and then I acted surprised when it optimized for the wrong thing. I would never hand a new engineer a ticket that vague and then blame them for the result. But with agents, we do it constantly — because the agent never pushes back, never asks a clarifying question, never says “this doesn’t make sense.” Silence looks like competence until the merge.

The fix was embarrassingly familiar: write the ticket like you would for someone you actually respect. What is the outcome? What is out of scope? What does “done” look like, and how will we know? The difference is that with a person, the conversation fills in the gaps. With an agent, the gaps stay gaps, and they get filled with confidence.

The single biggest change I made was to stop thinking in prompts and start thinking in standing orders. A prompt is a one-off instruction. A standing order is how a team operates when nobody is watching. Ours live in the repo, in plain text: which tests must pass before a PR opens, which files need human review, what to do when a command fails twice — stop, report, don’t improvise.

Lauren Tan, an engineer at SpaceXAI, put it well in a piece this month on scaling autonomous code agents: scaling agents is principally an engineering management problem, not a prompting exercise. Her framing is a trust curve. Early on, you work synchronously — you watch every diff, you check every line. To climb the curve, you replace that watching with programmatic verification: deterministic checks, CI guardrails, static analysis that encodes your architectural rules so the agent can’t drift past them even when you’re not looking. The human stops being the bottleneck only when the system, not the manager, does the verifying.

That matches what we’ve seen. The teams that get the most out of agents aren’t the ones with the cleverest prompts. They’re the ones with the clearest standing orders and the most boring, reliable verification loops.

You can’t coach an agent the way you coach a person. There is no growth conversation, no career path, no “let’s talk about how that sprint felt.” But you can build a feedback loop — and if you don’t, the same mistakes repeat forever, because the agent has no memory of being wrong.

Our loop is simple. Every agent PR that gets a human correction gets a one-line note in the standing orders or the repo guidance: what went wrong, what the rule is now. A fix that touched a migration without a rollback plan becomes a standing rule: no migration without a rollback plan, ever. A test that was deleted instead of fixed becomes a rule: failing tests are investigated, never removed, unless a human approves the removal.

This is slow, unglamorous work. It is also the entire job. Managing agents is mostly managing the system around them — the instructions, the verification, the feedback — because the agent itself doesn’t learn from Tuesday’s mistake unless you write the lesson down somewhere it will read on Wednesday.

There is one line I draw carefully. When an agent fails, I fix the system. When a person fails, I coach the person. Confusing the two is how you end up with either a team that resents the agents or a codebase full of agent-shaped workarounds.

If an engineer keeps overriding the agent’s guardrails, that’s a coaching conversation — about judgment, about why the guardrail exists. If the agent keeps producing work that needs heavy rework, that’s a systems problem — the standing orders are wrong, the verification is weak, or the task was too big to delegate in the first place. Blaming the agent is as useless as blaming the intern for a ticket you wrote badly.

The other mistake I see is managers using agents to avoid hard decisions. An agent can write the reorg plan, summarize the incident, or write the performance feedback. It cannot decide what kind of team you want to be. That is still the manager’s job, and delegating it to a model doesn’t make it go away — it just makes the decision worse and harder to trace.

Here’s what I can say honestly, from our own experience. The multi-agent orchestration we built took roughly half of our operations tasks off engineers’ plates, with human-in-the-loop approvals on anything that mattered, and developer productivity moved about 1.5x. That didn’t happen because the agents are brilliant. It happened because we treated them like a team: clear assignments, standing orders, verification that doesn’t depend on any one person’s attention, and a feedback loop that actually closes.

The engineers on my team didn’t get replaced. They moved up a level — from doing the toil to deciding what the toil should be and owning the judgment calls. The work that remains human is exactly the work that was always human: deciding what to build, what risk is acceptable, and what “good” looks like. The agents just made it impossible to pretend that work wasn’t the job all along.

The org chart of the future will have agents on it. The question isn’t whether that’s true — it’s whether you’ll manage them like a team or babysit them like a tool. One of those scales. The other one just makes you the bottleneck with better autocomplete.

AI vs. Engineers: What the Microsoft Buyouts Really Signal

#9572. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9571. Not Bacon: Give Grilled Cheese A Southern Twist With This Hearty Ingredient

Giving your grilled cheese a Southern twist doesn't mean you have to start using buttermilk biscuits and lard. Instead, you can use ham hocks, a seasoning meat that isn't always actually eaten but is always enjoyable.

The same thing that makes ham hocks delicious also makes them a bit difficult to use. Loaded with bone, connective tissue, and extremely tough meat, bringing out their flavor potential requires a lot of low-and-slow cooking. You may have more luck using smoked ham hocks for a deeper cure and smoke profile, though both smoked and raw hocks still require a long simmer to fully break down the tough collagen before transferring the meat to a sandwich. Regardless, adding shredded ham hock to grilled cheese gives you a tender, protein- and fat-laden ingredient that practically melts right alongside your gooey cheese.

Ham hocks are especially good when you "reuse" them. Cooking one dish with ham hocks and then using the meat in another lets you easily transfer complex flavors, a major tip for making any grilled cheese better. Hocks cooked in Southern-style collard greens adopt a perfectly moist texture and pick up acidity from vinegar and vegetable notes from the greens and onions. Similarly, ones cooked with black-eyed peas have a next-level creaminess, adopting earthy aromas to round out your sandwich. Still, if you want to preserve the smokiness of a fresh smoked ham hock, you can always simmer it for a couple of hours until the meat and skin fall apart, giving you a budget-friendly alternative to pulled pork.

Using ham hocks in your grilled cheese opens up new opportunities, since they're laden with fat and can make excellent use of leaner cheese varieties. Still, you should also consider what part of the hock to use, as some parts have more flavor than others and may require different ratios.

Typically, grilled cheese sandwiches rely on fatty, moisture-rich cheeses because they melt better than drier, aged varieties and carry that rich flavor profile. While you'll still want to use enough for a good texture, ham hocks provide plenty of decadence in their own right, so you can add a heavier sprinkle of Pecorino Romano or Parmigiano Reggiano, aged Gouda, or Manchego viejo. These underrated cheeses can cut through heavier fats more easily and are immediately noticeable even in small quantities, giving you a chance to add more complexity.

When you work with a smoked ham hock, you'll quickly notice how intense the skin's flavor is. Rich in fat and smoky flavor, this is a versatile ingredient you can mash into a spread for your bread, provided it's been properly simmered, or slice thinly and sprinkle in with shredded cheese. The meat directly under the skin is usually pinker and less potent, so it's a great choice if you're looking for more protein but not quite as much smoke. Meat from the top and bottom of the hock may offer a good middle ground, potentially holding more richness and smoke than interior meat but not quite as much as the skin, though this can vary depending on how the hock was smoked and prepared.

#9566. Upgrade Your Next Omelet With One Sweet Pantry Staple

Omelets are one of those dishes that feel made to be upgraded. While meats and vegetables go a long way toward something savory, going in a sweeter direction mixes things up and makes great use of one ingredient you probably already have on hand: honey.

A sweet omelet may sound a bit strange, but it's more common than you might think. Jelly omelets were a hit 100 years ago, and many Japanese folks love atsuyaki tamago, a rolled type of omelet that can be made with sweetened dashi stock. Using honey instead achieves a similar effect but gives you far more control over how your dish turns out. A drizzle over the top while it's still hot warms the honey, helping it spread more evenly and ensuring every bite is as sweet as you want it. Still, you can always mix a dash directly into the eggs, distributing the honey's sweetness throughout the omelet and potentially encouraging a bit of browning as it cooks.

For your first honey omelet, you may want to use something light, like honey made from orange blossom or clover nectar. These aren't overly intense and carry floral notes, and the addition of these aromas can make anyone's mouth water. If you're working with particularly rich eggs, especially duck eggs, you may want to use something with a bit more body, like wildflower or sunflower honey. These have the necessary depth of flavor to stand up to other ingredients and are great when you want a strong honey taste but not too much sweetness.

Honey can be a pretty potent ingredient, so adding too much extra sweetness with reduced tomatoes or caramelized onions can make your dish a bit too decadent in the morning. Instead, try going in the opposite direction, finding ways to add different kinds of saltiness, spice, and astringency for a complex blend of deliciousness.

A swicy flavor profile combines heat from capsaicin and sweetness from honey, both of which balance each other out and go great with eggs. Pork and honey also go together like peas and carrots, so a dollop of chorizo or spiced deli meats in an omelet brings umami, complexity, and harmonious flavors. This is a great opportunity to use hot honey as well, giving you more flexibility with other additions while still getting the same end result. Plus, spicy ingredients can add great color, improving the presentation of your dish to really wow your breakfast guests.

The best cheeses to add are usually sharp, salty, and earthy. Aged parmesan, extra-sharp cheddar, and really anything laden with salt crystals and pungency help balance the sweetness without overshadowing your honey's delicate flavors. Similarly, a bit of raw green onion can taste truly magnificent with honey and egg, but there's an emphasis on "a bit." Too much means you can't taste the honey, so try to aim for a miserly pinch at first and dial in your preference on subsequent attempts.

#9565. How I Made Codex CLI Resume Itself After Hitting a Usage Limit

International SEO & digital marketing manager. I grow brands with SEO, ads and AI, and build open-source tools. https://cybokron.com

International SEO & digital marketing manager. I grow brands with SEO, ads and AI, and build open-source tools. https://cybokron.com

International SEO & digital marketing manager. I grow brands with SEO, ads and AI, and build open-source tools. https://cybokron.com

If you run long tasks with the Codex CLI, you know the moment. You leave a refactor running, come back an hour later, and find the session stopped halfway because you hit the usage limit. Now you have to work out when the 5-hour window resets, come back at the right time, and type "continue" yourself. If the weekly limit ran out, the wait can last days, even though your account may hold reset credits that quietly expire unused.

This happened to me often enough that I built a small, free and open-source macOS menu bar app for it, called Cybokron Limit Guard. This post is less about the app and more about how it works: where Codex keeps the signals you need, why I avoided keystroke automation, and which guardrails I think every auto-continue tool needs.

Codex already exposes almost everything you need through two local sources.

The first is codex app-serverCodex's own local API. It speaks newline-delimited JSON-RPC, and account/rateLimits/read returns the 5-hour and weekly windows with their used percentage and reset time, plus a field called ordinaryUsageAllowed. It also lists the usage-limit reset credits on the account, each with an id, a status, and an expiry date. The protocol is marked as experimental, so I treat every field defensively.

The second is the session log. Each Codex session writes a JSONL "rollout" file under ~/.codex/sessions/. Every turn ends with a task_complete event, and when a turn was cut off by the limit, its error carries usage_limit_exceeded.

That single field is the difference between "the agent finished" and "the agent was interrupted". Finished turns, overload errors,s and aborted turns all look different, so the app can tell them apart without guessing.

My first idea was simple: read the reset time, set a timer, and send "continue" when it fires. That is not safe, and Codex's own schema says so: clients must not infer recovery from percentages or reset times.

So the reset time only schedules the first check. The real gate is ordinaryUsageAllowed == true from a fresh read that is less than 30 seconds old. If the value is false, Limit Guard keeps polling with back-off.

If it is null or cannot be decoded, the app does nothing. Polling also adapts: every five minutes normally, every minute once a window passes 90%, and every 30 seconds right after a reset.

The obvious way to "type continue" is to automate Terminal with AppleScript or synthetic key presses. I designed that path and then left it out of the first version. Typing into a terminal you can't fully see is risky: you might press Enter on an option picker or add text to a half-written prompt.

Codex already has a cleaner route. The Terminal session talks to a shared app-server daemon, and codex app-server proxy connects to that same daemon. A turn/start call with a thread ID starts a new turn in exactly that conversation, and the turn shows up in the user's Terminal tab. The turn keeps the thread's model, approval, and sandbox settings, because the app never overrides them. As a result, the app needs no Automation or Accessibility permission. If the daemon can't be reached, the app does not fall back to typing; it simply asks you to continue by hand.

Each continue carries a fresh clientUserMessageId. Within two minutes, the app looks for thatIDd or a new turn in the thread. If it can't confirm delivery, it marks the attempt as unconfirmed and never resends it on its own. You get a "Send again" button instead.

The message is written in the conversation's language. Apple's NaturalLanguage framework reads the last few real user messages, skips injected context such as AGENTS.md, and picks "continue" or "devam et." The table is editable, so you can add other languages.

Sending messages to an AI agent on someone's behalf can go wrong quietly, so most of the design is about knowing when to say no.

Some accounts receive usage-limit reset credits that expire. The app lists them with their expiry dates and puts the ones expiring within 24 hours first. A manual reset always asks for confirmation.

Automatic use is off by default. If you turn it on, the app spends one credit when the weekly limit reaches a threshold, 97% by default. It does this at most once per account every seven days, only while Codex is actually in use, and never when the weekly window would reset on its own within 12 hours. It always picks the credit that expires first.

A call that spends something needs idempotency. Before calling the consume endpoint, the app writes a ledger entry with a UUID idempotency key. If the call times out or the app crashes, it retries with the same key, so one intended reset can't turn into two. In the test suite, every spend path runs against a fake app-server, and the real endpoint is never called.

From recent samples, the app estimates how fast you are using each window and shows a line such as "at this pace the weekly limit runs out around Fri 14:00". A chart shows your daily token use for the last 7, 30, or 90 days, together with the history of both windows.

Everything stays on your Mac. The app reads session files only to detect stops and the conversation language. It never copies conversation text into its own files, never reads Codex's credential file,e and has no analytics. It talks only to Codex's local app-server and to GitHub for updates.

Version 0.1.1 supports the Codex CLI running in Terminal.app on macOS 14 Sonoma or later, with one universal build for Apple Silicon and Intel. You need to be signed into ChatGPT. (codex login). The interface is available in English and Turkish. Other terminals and editors, the Codex desktop app, other agents such as Claude Code, and multiple accounts are on the roadmap.

The app does not bypass any limit. It waits until Codex reports that usage is allowed again, or it uses a credit you already have. Automated use may still conflict with your platform's terms, so read them before you turn on automatic actions.

Limit Guard is written in Swift with AppKit and SwiftUI, has no third-party dependencies, and is notarized by Apple. It is free under the MIT license. You can download it from cybokron.com and read the source code on GitHub. Issues, ideas,s and pull requests are welcome.

Disclosure: I developed Cybokron Limit Guard. It is a free, open-source, independent tool and is not affiliated with or endorsed by OpenAI.

#9563. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.
