Good wishes for high school graduates should be grounded in encouragement. This is a time when everything feels new and a little uncertain. The best messages usually strike a balance between celebrating a significant achievement and acknowledging the emotional weight of leaving behind the familiar.

You might say something like: “You just accomplished something huge. Congratulations! And remember, it’s more than okay if the next step still feels a little uncertain.” This way, you’re honoring their hard work but also reminding them that they don’t need to have everything figured out yet.

Start by acknowledging the journey they’ve been on. College is typically full of academic pressure and personal growth. Let them know how proud you are of the person they’ve become.

You might say something like, “You’ve worked so hard, and I can’t wait to see what comes next. I’m so proud of the incredible person you are.”

Congratulate them, then add one kind thing about them. A few lines is plenty for a card. Here are some words for a graduation card, from short greetings to more personal notes:

"Congrats, grad! Your future is lucky to have you."

"Congratulations, graduate! I'm so proud of you."

"I've seen how much effort this took. I hope you feel so proud today."

"You kept going, even when things were hard. That says so much about who you are."

A good way to personalize a message is to reflect on what you admire about the graduate or how you’ve seen them evolve. Try naming something specific, like a moment they overcame something, or how they’ve impacted you.

Remember, you don’t need to write a long note. A short message like, “You’ve always led with compassion, and I admire that so much,” is powerful.

Funny graduation wishes are okay — just make sure the tone matches the moment. A light joke about student loans, caffeine dependency, or group projects gone wrong can land if it feels warm and comes from a place of love.

But as a rule of thumb, aim to avoid anything that pokes fun at their future or compares them to others.

A short message can still carry a lot of heart if it’s honest and specific. Here are a few examples that speak to a person’s strength and growth.

“You did it even when it felt impossible, and that says everything about how strong you are.”

“You poured your sweat and tears into this and earned every moment of it. I’m beyond proud.”

“I couldn’t be prouder of you and can’t wait to see what you do next.”

A good congratulations message for a graduate does two things. It says congratulations in plain words, and it names one thing you admire, like how hard they worked.

How you deliver it matters too. In person, a hug and “I’m so proud of you” mean a lot. In a card or text, you might write, “Congratulations on your graduation! I’ve loved watching you work toward this day.” Skip questions about what comes next. Many grads are still figuring that out, and today is for celebrating what they’ve done.

Start with congratulations, then add one thing you've loved watching her do. A line or two is plenty for a card. Here are short graduation messages for a granddaughter, whether she's finishing high school, college, or another program:

"So proud of you, my granddaughter. Congratulations on your graduation!"

"Watching you become who you are has been one of the great joys of my life. Congratulations, sweetheart."

"You're a very special young woman, and I'm so proud of all you've worked for. Congratulations!"

"You made it through high school, and I couldn't be prouder. Whatever comes next, you have my love."

"A college degree! Granddaughter, you've made me so proud. Congratulations."

"Being your grandma has been one of the best parts of my life. Congratulations, graduate!"

Congratulate the achievement and acknowledge the time it took. A doctorate often means years of research and writing, so mentioning that effort shows you see it. A line or two is enough. Here are a few short messages for a PhD or doctorate degree:

"Congratulations on completing your PhD. I've loved watching you work toward this day."

"You earned this doctorate through years of hard work. So proud of you!"

"Congratulations on your doctorate degree. I hope you take time to enjoy this one."

#9462. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

#9461. Artist Sun Xun’s new animated film was made over a decade from thousands of artworks

A scene from Sun Xun's Magic Atlas (2026) Courtesy the artist and π Animation Studio

A phrase cinephiles sometimes use to describe a visually beautiful movie is “every frame a painting”, but that is rarely more true than in Magic Atlas, a feature-length animation film by the Chinese painter Sun Xun, which was awarded a Special Jury Prize at the recently concluded Tokyo International Film Festival.

Sun spent ten years, on and off, working on the film, which he largely self-financed; rather than employ professional animators, he employed hundreds of art students (in one interview, he says 500 over the course of production) to produce individual frames, in a sort of supersized workshop model. Each frame has its own tactile quality, particularly in the sequences made in the unconventional animation medium of woodcut. When a shaft of line streams through a high window, piercing the blackness of an otherwise dark room, you can see the individual carving marks scored into the wood, which across several dozen frames dance and shimmer like the scales of a carp moving through a clear pond.

A scene from Sun Xun's Magic Atlas (2026) Courtesy the artist and π Animation Studio

Magic Atlas is a visual artist’s film, and as a storyteller, Sun thinks like a visual artist, proceeding by association, symbolism and dream logic. The magic atlas of the film’s title is a map to the mystic realms traversed by an explorer in a steampunk flying contraption. After the kaleidoscopic imagery of the film’s opening overture, he spends most of the film in one such world, a coal-mining kingdom called Luocha, where he is imprisoned on the eve of a magic festival. Maps are illegal in Luocha, as are memories. The authoritarian logic of the film is definitely allegorical, but the allegory is hard to pin down; the land’s emperor speaks of forced labour and industrial quotas, in perhaps a Maoist register, but the power behind the throne is an Orwellian cabal of anthropomorphised talking animals, who smoke cigars like colonial lords, and the state’s surveillance protocol is carried out by an army of mosquitos with cameras for heads—a swarm, if not a flock (or Flock).

In a manner similar to Chinese cinema’s emerging mystic-virtuoso Bi Gan, Sun is applying poetic ideas derived from Eastern spirituality about the oneness of all things, the many stories that are all one story. The film opens with a quote from Avatamsaka Sutra invoking “the past, the present, the future lying in the present”, and ends with a lengthy monologue, voiced by Sun himself, delivered by a hieroglyphic eagle. Its ideas about the transmigration of souls are mirrored in the mix of animation styles—the film spends most of its time in Luocha, which is rendered in monumental black-and-white woodcuts and illustrations reminiscent of Rockwell Kent, but also jumps at times to different styles that are each a world in and of themselves.

A scene from Sun Xun's Magic Atlas (2026) Courtesy the artist and π Animation Studio

There are homages to Salvador Dalí and Pieter Bruegel the Elder; a segment in riotous pastels with the Jazz Age voluptuousness of Reginald Marsh and a segment animated in crayon and magic marker by Sun’s Instagram followers during the Covid-19 pandemic; and segments informed by Sun’s own research into different styles of traditional Chinese art, including, he said in a post-screening interview, Dunhuang murals, Song dynasty painting, and multiple styles of calligraphy.

Exhibitions of Magic Atlas materials including woodcuts and concept art have shown at the Times Museum of Guangdong, and additional shows are planned in the United States (where Sun is represented by Sean Kelly Gallery). Sun received initial seed funding from Judith Neilson, the Australian philanthropist and founder of the Asian-focused White Rabbit Gallery, whose current show, up through November 15, includes Magic of Atlas – Luocha: An Infinite Journey, an 8ft-high, 52ft- long, 13-panel woodcut relief depicting images from the story in a scroll that can be stopped and started by the eyes of the viewer passing across the work—a static form of visual narrative that can be traced back to antiquity, long before still and moving images diverged.

#9460. This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.

The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.

The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.

Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.

They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.

Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.

Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.

The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.

The findings come from a new analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.

Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.

Dr David Field, the study’s first author, said:

“Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”

GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.

Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.

Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.

Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.

However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.

High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.

Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.

The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).

#9458. Comment | People mock Renoir, but painting joy is no easy feat

Purveyor of happiness: Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876) © RMN-Grand Palais/Mathieu Rabeau

“These young people are enjoying life, the beautiful weather, the morning sun shining through the foliage; what do they care about the rest of humanity?” So wrote Georges Rivière, writer and champion of Pierre-Auguste Renoir, of the French painter’s Dance at the Moulin de la Galette (1876), one of the highlights of Renoir and Love at London’s National Gallery (until 31 January 2027). “They are happy,” Rivière added, “and these are the words that come to mind of all who see this charming painting. None has given me more pleasure than this one.”

“Beautiful”, “happy”, “pleasure”—these terms sit uncomfortably with what John Elderfield, former curator at New York’s Museum of Modern Art, described to the painter Howard Hodgkin as “the modern attraction to difficulty”. Paul Perrin, co-curator of the Renoir show, writes in its catalogue that the “blissful couples and air of happiness” in Renoir’s 1860s to 1880s paintings have made them “immensely popular” yet also prompted “contempt for their apparent lack of complexity and depth”. His assessment was newly confirmed by the critic Eddy Frankel, writing recently in The Guardian: “I’ve hated his work for decades.” For him, Renoir only appeals “when his nudes look like a super-psychedelic, ultra-horny version of Rubens”.

Renoir himself understood that milder emotions irked critics. “It’s hard to get people to admit that a painting can be great painting and still be happy,” he wrote. But love, as framed in this show, has multiple forms, among them empathy. Specialists suggest that Renoir was not ignorant of the “anguished or miserable” elements of life that Perrin describes as being essential to many conceptions of modernity. When Rivière wrote about young people dancing in ignorance of the rest of humanity, he didn’t need to add that happiness can be fleeting and is often most intensely felt at its briefest.

Renoir’s Dance in the Country (1883) © RMN-Grand Palais (Musée d’Orsay)/Hervé Lewandowski

The writings of Baudelaire, and the paintings of Renoir’s peers like Degas and Manet, tell us how visible hardship would have been at the time. And Renoir, unlike those two peers, grew up in working-class Paris, so had lived experience that gave him, as Rivière wrote, “a keen sense of pity” for the poverty of “Montmartre families”. But Renoir clearly felt that if he did want to create great, happy art, he had to avoid troubling subject matter: “There are enough annoying things in life for us not to make more of them,” he said.

Another factor in Renoir’s commitment to joy and play was his deep admiration for what he saw as the golden age of French painting: the Rococo. As Mary Morton writes in the Renoir and Love catalogue, the work of artists like Jean-Antoine Watteau and Jean-Honoré Fragonard “embodied graceful pleasure and a harmonious relationship between the human figure and nature”.

Renoir shares this infatuation with Rococo with a contemporary artist who I think has come closer than anyone else to creating a great art of happiness: Ragnar Kjartansson, whose exhibition Weekdays in Arcadia opens at the Goodwood Art Foundation in Chichester this month (26 November-12 April 2027). Kjartansson told me in 2017 that his fascination with the period lies in the “contrast of really intellectual minds and… silly-billy nothingness”. At Goodwood, he will show No Tomorrow (2022), a video installation that extends his 2017 dance collaboration with choreographer Margrét Bjarnadóttir and composer Bryce Dessner. When I saw the original ballet, in which a group of female performers dressed in jeans and white T-shirts dance with acoustic guitars for the duration of the piece, one moment made me instantly grin: arranged in a grid, every other dancer would take it in turns to leap into the air while the performer next to them stood still, prompting a joyous effect of corporeal effervescence. Kjartansson told me he and Bjarnadóttir felt No Tomorrow was “a Watteau painting in disguise”.

Kjartansson’s most famous piece, The Visitors (2012), a video installation in which he and his friends perform a song in different rooms of a half-derelict mansion in New York State, provokes a similarly ecstatic response from its viewers. But Kjartansson was conscious, perhaps with the reputation of artists like Renoir and of the Rococo period in mind, that he was “in danger of becoming the feel-good artist”. And indeed, part of what makes him such a compelling figure is that the light of his work always comes with copious amounts of shade. At Goodwood, he is interested in “the idea of encountering monuments to sorrow and shakiness in the woodlands”. And yet, I suspect he will find ways to make us smile amid the melancholy.

Achieving joy in art is difficult. Perhaps the most perceptive observer of this fact is one of Renoir’s artistic heirs, Henri Matisse, who spoke of the anguish behind the pleasure in his work: “this happiness, this light and this serene wisdom that [have] seemingly become mine are sometimes earned through the harshness of adversity”. Matisse and, I think, Renoir—like Kjartansson—knew that achieving happiness is a deadly serious business.

#9457. How to stop emotional flooding from disrupting your relationships

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

The argument started with the dishes. Now you're saying something you know you’ll regret. Two minutes ago, you were mildly annoyed. Now your heart is pounding, and you can barely hear your partner over the noise in your own head.

This is emotional flooding, and it can happen to anyone. It isn’t a character flaw, and it doesn’t mean you're bad at relationships. When emotions run hot, the level-headed version of you can seem to vanish.

Flooding tends to show up when you're close to someone and the stakes feel personal. Fortunately, if you spot the signs early, you can keep an argument from turning into a blowup. Ahead, we’ll explore the science behind emotional flooding and how to calm yourself when it hits.

Emotional flooding is a state of overwhelm during a heated moment, usually a conflict. The term comes from John Gottman, PhD, who describes flooding as the point when you’re so overloaded that you can't take in new information, solve the problem, or hear the person in front of you.

Gottman and his colleague Robert Levenson studied couples at the University of Washington. As partners argued, they tracked physical signals like heart rate. Couples whose bodies showed higher arousal during conflict tended to grow less satisfied with their relationship over the following years.

Flooding feels different from person to person, so you may notice some of these signs but not others. Here's what to look for:

Racing heart: Your pulse climbs, and you feel your heartbeat in your chest or throat.

Fast, shallow breathing: Your breaths come quick and tight, and a full inhale feels out of reach.

Heat and tension: Your face flushes, and your jaw or shoulders tighten.

Tunnel vision: Your thinking narrows, and the other person’s words get hard to follow.

Urge to fight or flee: You want to raise your voice or leave, and it feels difficult to hold back.

Numbness or blankness: Your thoughts freeze, and you feel disconnected from the conversation.

Emotional flooding involves the amygdala, the part of your brain built to detect danger and keep you safe. When it senses a threat, it triggers the stress response and releases a surge of hormones that put your body on high alert. Adrenaline and norepinephrine speed up your heart rate and pull your focus toward the threat. That narrowed focus is part of why listening gets so hard.

In an everyday disagreement, there’s usually no physical danger, but your brain can still treat a raised voice or a difference of opinion as a threat, setting off the same alarm and the same rush of anger.

In close relationships, flooding may get extra fuel. Arguments can touch things that matter deeply to you, like feeling respected or safe. Old wounds and fear of where the fight might lead can pile on top of the present moment.

A note on relationships that don’t feel safe: This article is about everyday arguments, not abuse. If a raised voice or a pattern of control leaves you afraid of your partner, that fear isn’t a false alarm. Self-soothing isn’t the tool for this, and your safety comes first. You can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline any time at 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.

You can't always stop flooding before it starts, but you can help your body calm down once you realize it’s happening. Then, when you feel settled enough to think clearly again, you can gently return to the conversation. The tips below follow that order: calm your body first, then come back and repair. Try the ones that fit the moment, and skip any that don’t feel right for you.

The moment you notice your heart racing or your thoughts scrambling, tell yourself “this is flooding.” Naming it reminds you that the feeling is physical and temporary. That bit of awareness gives you room to choose your next move instead of reacting on autopilot.

💙 Try the Full Sensory Awareness meditation on the Calm app.

A longer exhale engages your parasympathetic nervous system, the part of your nervous system that helps you rest and settle down.

In one study, people who practiced cyclic sighing (also known as the physiological sigh), a breathing pattern of two quick inhales and one long exhale, reported bigger mood improvements than those who practiced mindfulness meditation.

If breathing exercises feel uncomfortable, skip ahead to the next tip.

💙 Press play on the Breathe to Calm Down session on Calm.

When you're flooded, stepping away can help you collect yourself before you talk things through. Tell your partner you need a break and that you’ll come back, so they don’t feel abandoned mid-conflict.

According to Gottman's research, it can take at least 20 minutes for your body to calm back down, so give yourself enough time. If you can’t leave the room, even a few minutes of silence can help.

Your body often responds to physical cues faster than logic. Use your time-out to splash cold water on your face or step outside for a few minutes of fresh air. Either one can help slow your heart rate.

💙 If anger is running hot, listen to Calm’s Investigating Anger session.

Flooding releases stress hormones that prepare your body for action. A brisk walk, or any gentle movement that suits you, gives that energy somewhere to go instead of letting it build.

💙 Explore Dr. Eric López's Walk Away Stress series on Calm.

Once it feels calmer, return to your partner. You don't have to solve everything right away. A short repair can open the door to trying again.

Try: “I got overwhelmed earlier. Can we try again?”

Gottman’s work suggests that how couples repair after conflict is a key predictor of long-term satisfaction, often more telling than how often they fight.

💙 Learn how couples meditation can strengthen your relationship.

Emotional flooding is feeling so overwhelmed during a conflict or another intense moment that you can’t think clearly or listen. The term comes from psychologist John Gottman's research on couples.

A common example of emotional flooding is a tense meeting with your boss, when your heart starts pounding and your mind goes blank. It can also happen at home, like when a conversation with a family member or partner escalates.

💙 Check out how to deal with a conflict at work.

Emotional flooding is a surge of intense emotion in a specific moment, while emotional dysregulation is ongoing difficulty managing emotions across a range of situations. Flooding can be one sign of dysregulation, but if it happens now and then, that doesn’t necessarily mean you have a pattern of dysregulation.

Emotional flooding can be more common and more intense for people with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder). Studies show that trouble managing emotions is a core part of ADHD in adults. With ADHD, you may flood more often or take longer to calm down.

If flooding feels constant or unmanageable, a doctor can help you figure out what’s behind it.

💙 Learn what ADHD shutdown is and how to manage it.

You can stop being emotionally flooded by giving your body time to settle before you continue the conversation. Take a break of at least 20 minutes, and try long exhales, cold water on your face, or a brisk walk. When you feel more grounded, give the conversation another try.

Mindfulness can help with emotional flooding because it trains you to notice early signs, such as a racing heart or a tight jaw, before they build. Over time, that gives you a chance to pause instead of react in hard moments.

Try to practice mindfulness when you’re calm, with short breathing exercises or guided meditation, so the skill is there when you need it.

#9456. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

4. Watson P, Norman SB, Maguen S, Hamblen J. Moral injury in health care workers. Accessed January 4, 2021. https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/moral_injury_hcw.asp

5. Shahrour G, Dardas LA. Acute stress disorder, coping self-efficacy and subsequent psychological distress among nurses amid COVID-19. J Nurs Manag. 2020;28(7):1686-1695. doi:10.1111/jonm.13124

6. Lahav Y. Psychological distress related to COVID-19 — The contribution of continuous traumatic stress. J Affect Disord. 2020;277:129-137. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.141

7. Stovall M, Hansen L, van Ryn M. A critical review: moral injury in nurses in the aftermath of a patient safety incident. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2020;52(3):320-328. doi:10.1111/jnu.12551

8. Pappa S, Ntella V, Giannakas T, Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Katsaounou P. Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and insomnia among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Brain Behav Immun. 2020;88:901-907. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2020.05.026

9. Pietrzak RH, Feingold JH, Feder A, Charney DS, Peccoralo L, Southwick SM, Ripp J. Psychological resilience in frontline health care workers during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;82(1):20l13749. doi:10.4088/JCP.20l13749

10. Krystal JH, Alvarado J, Ball SA, et al. Mobilizing an institutional supportive response for healthcare workers and other staff in the context of COVID-19: the Yale experience. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:12-18. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.11.005

11. Park ER, Sylvia LG, Streck JM, et al. Launching a resiliency group program to assist frontline clinicians in meeting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic: results of a hospital-based systems trial. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:111-112. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.10.005

12. Kameno Y, Hanada A, Asai D, et al. Individual psychotherapy using psychological first aid for frontline nurses at high risk of psychological distress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2021;75(1):25-27. doi:10.1111/pcn.13170.

13. Shanafelt T, Ripp J, Trockel M. Understanding and addressing sources of anxiety among health care professionals during the COVID-19 pandemic. JAMA. 2020;323(21):2133-2134. doi:10.1001/jama.2020.5893

#9455. 5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is important for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

#9453. Clinical Challenge: Cough, Fever, in Person Who Vapes

A 16-year-old adolescent presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of vomiting, tactile fevers, and a mild headache that went away 2 days earlier. The patient denies any abdominal or flank pain, dysuria, diarrhea, or other complaints. When specifically questioned, she acknowledges a slight cough but has no shortness of breath or chest pain.

The patient’s vital signs are normal except for an elevated temperature (100.3 °F) and a pulse rate 133 beats per minute. Initial physical examination is otherwise normal with no rash, tonsillar exudate, rales, murmur, flank tenderness, or other abnormality. Chest radiographs (Figure 1-2) and blood work are ordered. Laboratory results are within normal range except for an elevated white blood cell count (19,000/μL). Pregnancy and COVID-19 PCR tests are negative.

Can you diagnose this condition? What is the most important medical history question to ask?

#9452. ‘I’m lucky to have grown up around artists’: Cora Sheibani on her path to becoming a jeweller

Cora Sheibani wearing jewellery from her own collections: a bronze bracelet (from Pottering Around collection), Renaissance earrings in platinum and a sapphire facet ring in 18K red gold (both from Facets & Forms Collection)

Art of Luxury magazine, published twice per year by The Art Newspaper, explores how grande marque fashion, jewellery, travel and lifestyle interact with artists, the art market and the museums and heritage sector.

The jeweller Cora Sheibani lives in London and works from a small studio in Mayfair. She was raised in the art world—her father was the celebrated Swiss dealer Bruno Bischofberger, who collaborated with artists including Jean-Michel Basquiat, Andy Warhol and Francesco Clemente. As a dyslexic, Cora did not embrace reading as a child, but now she explains why it is her window on the world.

For me, luxury is about having time. As you get older, and as the world gets faster, there’s never enough of it. In an ideal world I would travel more, both for work and for pleasure; and visit exhibitions, galleries and museums. But I also have a son who needs a lot of my attention—he is very autistic, with severe ADHD—and so I travel through books, and reading has become a way to experience culture, art and creativity.

I’m lucky to have grown up around artists and people who didn’t follow the conventional path. Francesco Clemente is a close family friend, and his daughters are more like my cousins. We’re close to the Schnabel family; Jean Tinguely was my sister’s godfather. So even though I barely read as a child—it was just too hard—I made myself study liberal arts before I became a jeweller. Only after university I started reading German literature. It’s my mother language, after all.

I’ve always loved jewellery. When I was 15, I worked in my parents’ gallery over the summer, and spent half my earnings on two rings, both bronze, one Greek, one Roman. Now I work primarily with gold: at first it was because yellow is my favourite colour, but you also learn that gold is the friendliest metal to handle.

It was hard to be taken seriously as a jeweller at the beginning. People thought it was a hobby, and I really had to be patient and persevere—that’s something I can do, that dyslexia taught me. Now I’m incredibly proud of my work and how successful the business has become.

Jewellery books and especially exhibition catalogues are a real inspiration. An essay by Amin Jaffer in the catalogue for Joyaux Dynastiques, a show at the Hôtel de la Marine in Paris last year of royal jewels, explained the meaning of a particular kind of nine-gem Indian jewel. It really helped me with a commission I’d just received from a client for a piece using nine different coloured stones.

I buy some early editions from Shapero Rare Books in Mayfair—I pass it every time I go from the gym to the studio and can’t resist taking a look. I just finished reading Crime and Punishment by Fyodor Dostoyevsky in its first English translation by Frederick Whishaw. It’s very rare, a real collector’s item. It’s generally thought that translations have improved, but there’s something special about reading a contemporaneous one. It’s a rich experience that takes you back in time.

Once a month, I get together with my book club. There’s only three of us, and we don’t all have to read the same book. Instead, we talk about what we are each reading. We meet, usually on a Friday morning, at Daria Buchman’s house, and have a breakfast of scrambled eggs. Daria, with her husband Dimitry, sponsors the International Booker Prize, so she is really on top of every new novel. She hadn’t read Beloved by Toni Morrison, though. I’d read three works that talked about slavery from different regional angles—Beloved, Crooked Plow by Itamar Vieira Junior and Ben Okri’s The Last Gift of the Master Artists—and recommended to my group they did the same. You begin to understand a bit better how the lives of people from one continent evolved in such different (and at times similar) ways. On the other hand, Daria made me read the wonderful Wuthering Heights. I wouldn’t have done it if she hadn’t insisted.

Frédéric Boucheron created the first necklace without a clasp so that women could put it on unaided

#9451. 36 Healthy Fall Dinners With All The Cozy

Healthy and nourishing fall dinners that are super cozy, too! Some of my favorite bowls, salads, soups, and more!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 18, 2026

Fall dinners are here, and honestly, this is the kind of food I wait for all year. Steamy bowls, creamy sauces, roasted veggies, cozy spices, and meals that make the whole house smell amazing. These healthy fall recipes bring all the sweater-weather comfort while still being nourishing enough for an everyday weeknight!

To call out a few of my all-time favorites from this list:

Nourishing food should still feel generous, cozy, and completely delicious, and these dinners are it!

Roasted sweet potatoes topped with creamy chipotle sauce, spicy ground chicken, avocado, cilantro, and pickled onion. My family loves them!

I love this Kale Apple Salad! Kale, brussels sprouts, rosemary cashews, apples, fried bread cheese, crispy shallots, and crisp apple maple dressing!

Silky carrot soup topped with spiced ground beef and toasty pine nuts! Bright, savory, warming, all the best things!

Amazingly creamy, saucy chickpea curry served over rice with a dollop of chili crisp and a side of cucumber salad. Ready in 20 minutes!

One of my family’s favorite easy dinners that works SO well for meal prep! Sweet potatoes and ground beef get dolloped with a creamy high protein street corn style dip that is bonkers delicious.

Detox Crockpot Lentil Soup – a clean and simple soup made with onions, garlic, carrots, olive oil, squash, and LENTILS! Super healthy and easy to make.

The BEST Grain Bowl! Roasted root vegetables, earthy grains, dried fruit, dark leafy greens, buttery goat cheese, and lusciously creamy balsamic dressing.

Coconut Curry Salmon! Broiled salmon with a salty-sweet spice rub, creamy coconut curry sauce, and steamy rice to soak it all up.

These tempeh bowls are a true fall favorite! Massaged kale, sweet potatoes, roasty marinated maple-mustard tempeh, crunchy apple, and an unexpected pile of briney sauerkraut.

Lemongrass, ginger, shallot, and the brightness of lime! These broth bowls have got it all – luscious broth, fluffy rice, protein, and fresh herbs.

Saucy shredded chicken, yellow rice, pickled onions, greens, and cilantro pesto on top. It’s a flavor and color delight!

We are living our best bowl life this week. Seasoned sweet potato wedges and chicken meatballs or rotisserie chicken all piled onto a plate with a little puddle of punchy green avocado mojo sauce. Yes, wow, repeat.

This 7-Layer Beet Salad is a stunner! Studded with cooked beets, supremed oranges, chopped pistachios, creamy truffle ricotta, and a bit of fresh mint. So fresh, so good!

These House Favorite Brussels Sprouts are the best side veg and are speckled with bright bursts of cranberries and nutty walnuts. The perfect addition to any meal!

#9450. This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, said:

“A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”

The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

The memory findings were more complicated.

Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in new information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9449. 101 fun questions for your kids to laugh, talk, and connect

Have you ever asked your child what they did at school only to be told, “I don’t remember…”?

Many kids have a magical ability to give the least amount of detail possible when asked a direct question. It’s almost like they’re professionally trained in the art of dodging conversation.

The thing is, kids actually do want to talk. You just have to ask the right questions: ones that spark their imagination, make them laugh, or invite them to share something meaningful on their terms.

So, meet them where they are. Instead of the same old, “How was your day?” (which, let’s be honest, will never yield a thrilling response), try questions that make them pause and think for a moment. This way, you’re not prying information out of them, you’re building a habit of open conversation, one fun question at a time.

Ask them in the car, at bedtime, over breakfast, or whenever your kid is in a chatty mood. You might be surprised at what they share — and the hilarious, heartwarming, or even unexpectedly deep conversations that follow.

Laughter is one of the easiest ways to connect with your child (and can boost your mental health too). These offbeat, ridiculous questions will get them giggling while giving you a glimpse into their wonderfully weird little minds.

Would you rather have a banana for a nose or popcorn for ears? Kids love absurd choices, and these “would you rather” questions are a surefire way to spark hilarious debates.

Would you rather have spaghetti for hair or marshmallows for fingers?

Would you rather live in a house made of chocolate or a castle made of cheese?

Would you rather always talk in rhymes or only be able to whisper?

Would you rather ride a roller coaster that never ends or a Ferris wheel that goes super fast?

Would you rather have a pet dragon or a pet unicorn?

Ever wonder what your backpack thinks about your daily routine? These questions help kids think outside the box — and maybe appreciate their favorite objects a little more.

If your socks could talk, what would they say about your feet?

If your toothbrush had feelings, how would it feel about its job?

If your toys threw a party while you were sleeping, what would they do?

If your backpack could complain, what would it say?

If animals could talk to you, which one do you think would be the funniest?

What if the moon really was made of cheese? These questions let kids build wild, imaginary worlds where anything is possible.

If you could invent a new holiday, what would it be called and how would we celebrate?

If your shadow had a mind of its own, what do you think it would do?

If you could make one silly law that everyone had to follow, what would it be?

If you had a magic remote that could pause or rewind real life, when would you use it?

What’s better than food? Food-related nonsense! These questions are perfect for mealtime giggles.

What’s the silliest pizza topping combination you can think of?

If you could turn any food into a superhero, which one would you pick and why?

If vegetables could talk, which one would be the grumpiest?

If you ate only dessert for an entire day, which treats would you choose?

If you could invent a new ice cream flavor, what would it be?

💙 Why not incorporate some silly moves into your kids day with Mel Mah’s Working Out the Wiggles session?

Forget the usual “What’s your favorite color?” These questions dig a little deeper into what makes your child them — their dreams, their interests, and how they see the world.

Who are they, really? These questions help kids define what makes them special. Who knows? They might even surprise themselves with their answers.

What’s something you love doing that makes you feel really happy?

If you could rename yourself, what would you want to be called?

What’s one thing that makes you feel really proud of yourself?

If you had to describe yourself in three words, what would they be?

Every kid has dreams. These questions encourage them to think big.

If you could have any job in the world when you grow up, what would it be?

If you could live anywhere in the world, where would it be?

If you could suddenly have super-skill, what would it be?

If you could invent something to make life easier, what would it do?

What’s something you dream about doing one day?

What’s school really like? What do they wish adults understood? These questions help you see the world through their eyes.

If you could be principal of your school for a day, what rules would you change?

What’s one thing about school that you really like?

What’s one thing about school you wish was different?

What’s one thing you wish adults understood about being a kid?

Forget the usual “favorite color” and “favorite food” questions — these favorites are a little more unexpected.

If you could only listen to one song forever, what would it be?

If you could only watch one movie over and over again, which one would you pick?

If you could only eat three foods for a year, what would they be?

What book should everyone read at least once?

If you were a baseball player, what song would play when you came up to bat?

These questions help kids think outside the box and explore new ideas — without it feeling like homework.

What if everything was upside down? What if people lived in the ocean? These questions let kids stretch their creativity and invent a world of their own.

If you could switch lives with any fictional character, who would it be?

If you could time travel, would you rather visit the past or the future?

If you could build a brand-new planet, what would it be like?

If you could talk to any historical figure, who would you pick and what would you ask?

If you could live in any book or movie world, which one would you choose?

Kids love hypotheticals, especially ridiculous ones. These questions tap into their curiosity and creativity.

If aliens landed in our backyard, what would be the first thing you’d say to them?

If you could talk to animals, what’s the first thing you’d ask them?

If you could change one thing about the world, what would it be?

If you could be invisible for a day, what would you do?

If you could wake up with a superpower, which one would you want?

Kids are natural philosophers. Sometimes, they just need the right question to get them going.

What’s something you’ve always been curious about but never asked?

If you could solve one big mystery in the world, what would it be?

If you could design your dream school, what classes would you add?

What’s something that happens in nature that seems magical to you?

What do you think is the coolest invention ever made?

These questions encourage kids to see things in a new way, whether it’s about themselves, the world, or the future.

What’s something small that can make a big difference?

What’s a time when you changed your mind about something?

If you could ask the president one question, what would it be?

What’s one way kids can change the world?

What’s something you wish you knew how to do?

Kids may not always have the words to explain their feelings, but these thoughtful questions help create a safe space for them to share what’s in their hearts. The Feelings Wheel can be a good visual aid for this too.

Sometimes, kids just need the right words to talk about how they feel. These questions give them a way to open up.

What’s something that made you feel really happy this week?

What’s a time when you felt really proud of yourself?

What’s something that always makes you feel loved?

What’s a time when you felt really brave?

What’s something you wish people knew about you?

It’s not always easy to talk about the hard stuff, but these questions can help kids express their feelings in a safe way.

What’s something that helps you feel better when you’re sad?

What’s a time when something felt really hard, but you got through it?

What’s one thing that makes you feel nervous?

What’s something you do when you’re feeling frustrated?

What’s a time when someone helped you feel better?

Friends are a huge part of kids’ lives — these questions help them reflect on what friendship means to them.

What do you think makes someone a good friend?

What’s one way you like to show kindness to others?

What do your friends do to make you feel special?

What’s something you love doing with your family?

If you could plan the perfect day with your best friend, what would you do?

Slowing down and noticing the good things is a skill kids can carry with them for life. These questions make space for reflection.

What’s something you’re really grateful for today?

What’s a small thing that makes a big difference in your day?

What’s a memory that always makes you smile?

What’s something you love about yourself?

What’s one thing you want to remember about being a kid when you’re older?

These questions are designed to spark deeper connections and create shared experiences — because the best conversations are about connecting.

Every family has inside jokes, traditions, and funny moments. These questions bring them to the surface.

If you could plan a dream family vacation, where would we go?

What’s something funny that has happened in our family?

What’s a meal we should cook together soon?

If we could create a secret family handshake, what would it look like?

Remember that time we all got soaked in the rain? Or the time you laughed so hard you snorted? These questions help relive the best moments.

What’s something we’ve done together that made you laugh really hard?

What’s the silliest story I’ve ever told you?

What’s one thing we should do more often as a family?

What’s next for our family? These questions invite kids to dream up exciting adventures — real or imagined.

If we could go on a wild adventure tomorrow, what would we do?

What’s a hobby or activity you’d love for us to try together?

If you could design the perfect family game night, what would we play?

If we could time travel together, what era would we visit?

If we started a family business, what would we sell?

Every family has its own kind of magic. These questions bring it out in unexpected ways.

If our family had a theme song, what would it be?

If we could invent a new family tradition, what would it be?

If you could give everyone in our family a superpower, what would they be?

If every member of our family was an animal, what would it be?

What’s a way we can make someone else’s day better together?

What’s one thing you want me to always remember about you?

💙 Mel Mah’s Kids Bedtime Routine can help you all wind down in a peaceful way, together.

The best questions to ask kids are open-ended, playful, and relevant to their world. Instead of asking, “Did you have a good day?”—which almost always leads to a dead-end answer—try something that sparks their imagination or invites storytelling, like “What was the funniest thing that happened today?” or “If you could switch places with your teacher for a day, what would you do?” Kids are much more likely to engage when a question feels fun, unexpected, and free of pressure.

Kids love absurdity, so the weirder and wackier the question, the better. Offbeat questions tap into their creativity, making conversation feel more like a game than a chore.

Silly questions are also a great way to bond, especially when you play along. If your kid tells you they’d rather ride a roller coaster that never stops over a Ferris wheel that goes super fast, ask why and join in the fun by sharing your own ridiculous answer.

Laughter is a powerful connector, and sometimes the most unexpected conversations start with a totally goofy question.

For 6-year-olds, short questions about things they can picture work best. Silly choices and pretend play go over well. Try “What would you name a pet cloud?” or “If your stuffed animals had jobs, what would they be?” Many of the funny questions above fit this age, especially the “would you rather” and “If your stuff could talk” lists. Ask one question at a time, since young kids can lose the thread when you ask two at once.

Which question to ask depends on what you want from the chat. If you want laughs, pick a “would you rather” or other funny question. If you want to know your child better, choose from the get-to-know list. For big feelings, try the emotional expression questions. When you’re not sure, start silly to help them relax, then move to a deeper one.

Kids spend a lot of their day being told what to do—sit still, follow directions, finish their homework—so having a space where they get to lead the conversation is powerful. Asking fun and engaging questions gives them a chance to express themselves, think creatively, and feel heard without any right or wrong answers. It also helps build communication skills, emotional intelligence, and a sense of connection with you.

Beyond that, these questions create opportunities for everyday bonding. A quick chat in the car or during dinner can turn into a meaningful moment of connection. The more kids feel like their thoughts and ideas are valued, the more likely they are to open up — not just about the silly stuff but about the big things, too.

The key to getting good answers is making the conversation feel natural, not forced. If you ask a question and get a one-word response, don’t panic — sometimes kids just need a little extra space to warm up. Try following up with, “Tell me more!” or sharing your own answer first to get the ball rolling. If they see that you’re genuinely interested (and willing to be a little silly yourself), they’ll be more likely to engage.

Also, be thoughtful about your timing. Some kids open up more when they’re relaxed—like at bedtime or when you’re doing an activity together—while others chat more when they’re distracted, like in the car. If they’re tired, hungry, or mid-screen time, you might not get much out of them. But if you catch them in the right moment, you might just unlock a goldmine of thoughts, ideas, and hilarious kid logic.

The best time to ask kids questions is when they’re naturally more open to conversation — when they feel safe, relaxed, and not pressured to respond. For some kids, that’s during bedtime, when they’re winding down and their thoughts start to flow. For others, it’s in the car, when there’s no pressure for eye contact and they can talk freely. Meal times, walks, or even while playing with Legos can also be great moments to slip in a fun question.

Trying to force deep conversation right after school when their brain is fried or when they’re engrossed in a game or show usually won’t work. Instead, look for organic, low-pressure moments when chatting feels easy. And remember, it’s not about when you ask, it’s about showing up consistently so that when they are ready to talk, they know you’ll be there to listen.

#9448. Apple Crisp

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on September 29, 2026

Made this last night, and it’s now the whole family’s favorite apple crisp. Easy to make and very, very delicious!

I jotted this apple crisp recipe into the notes app in my phone several years ago, and I return to it every fall.

Jammy, cinnamon-scented apples baked under a heavy (and I do mean heavy) blanket of buttery crumble.

I remember first making this in our old kitchen for a late-October dinner party – I made wild rice soup and apple cider old fashioneds (unreal), and someone pulled out the guitar just as the smell of apple crisp was floating from the oven. Absolutely charmed. I obviously bonded with this specific apple crisp that night and it has been with me ever since.

Why it’s good, if you ask me: the caramely apple layer underneath gets properly jammy, the topping gets properly crisp – just enough to provide contrast, AND, and, and, where the two layers melt together in the middle is just pure fall magic. Soft, buttery, and delicious.

Apple crisp in general is very simple, and this one feels rustic, almost, especially if you make it in a cast iron pan, which I usually do. Is she making apple crisp or is she living out her dreams from Little House on the Prairie on a chilly fall night? We’ll never know.

Toss apples with sugar, cinnamon, and flour. This photo shows apples that have been thinly sliced on a mandoline. You can also dice them! Both delicious.

I stir it up with a spoon or fork, and then bring it together into crumbles with my hands.

It’ll turn into a beautiful golden crumble with a layer of jammy apples underneath.

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

My one-and-only apple crisp recipe! Tender jammy honeycrisp apples under a blanket of buttery brown sugar oat topping. The perfect fall treat!

This can work with or without peeling the apples. Personally, I don’t peel the apples – I am lazy, and I just can’t be bothered to mess with what is already a perfectly good fruit. The peels cook down the same way the apples do, so they become soft and unobtrusive in the apple crisp.

#9446. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

– it will make the broth a bit thicker / starchier, and I prefer a silky, light broth

– the noodles will be more at risk of overcooking and getting mushy since they continue to sit in the hot liquid

– it doesn’t keep as well as leftovers (I prefer to just freeze the broth on its own)

– the experience of pouring the broth over the noodles is really fun. 🙂
